figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: Token analysis, BFT, and applications. a : Semantic composition of low-confidence tokens inside Group A (sparse-low) and Group B (dense-low). b : 4096-token trace illustrating one sparse-low window (Group A) and one dense-low window (Group B). c : BFT applies token- and sample-level loss adjustments. d : BFT-generated biomedical profiles are encoded by a text embedding model for downstream representation tasks.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure combining plots, schematic workflows, and model architecture.

- **Panel a:** Bar chart of **token composition (%)** comparing **Group A sparse-low windows** and **Group B dense-low windows**. Categories include interchangeable expressions, common vocabulary, biomedical entities, and causal/reasoning chains. Group A appears enriched for interchangeable/common vocabulary tokens, while Group B appears enriched for biomedical entities and causal/reasoning chains.
- **Panel b:** Line/trace plot of **4096-token response confidence**, with highlighted windows: **Window A sparse low-confidence** and **Window B dense low-confidence**. Zoom-in plots show token confidence patterns in each window, with local mean confidence annotated.
- **Panel c:** Workflow schematic for **Balanced Fine-Tuning (BFT)**. It contrasts token-level weighting for sparse low-confidence tokens in Group A with sample-level or trajectory-level weighting for dense low-confidence Group B, aiming to stabilize gradients and reduce overfitting.
- **Panel d:** Model pipeline diagram: an **LLM** plus **biomedical trajectory** undergoes **BFT** to produce **LLM-BFT**, which generates descriptions of biomedical entities and maps them through a text embedding model into an embedding space.

Main visible finding: low-confidence token regions are separated into sparse and dense patterns, with different token compositions, and the proposed BFT strategy weights them differently to improve biomedical entity description/embedding behavior.

Multi-panel quantitative plot figure with experiment results. Panel **a** shows grouped point/error-bar plots of **Score** across model sizes **14B, 32B, 70B**, split into **Axis** and **Theme** task categories. X-axis labels include biomedical/scientific concept categories such as dataset-related and semantic/theme categories. Legend compares methods: **Base**, **SFT**, **DFT**, **BFT-sample**, **BFT-token**, and **BFT**.

Panel **b** shows line plots of **Regent-1 Score** versus **Model Size** for benchmarks **MsigDB**, **NeST**, and **GeneOntology**, with separate rows/conditions and the same method legend. A green dashed horizontal reference line labeled **GeneAgent** is shown.

Main visible finding: **BFT variants, especially BFT/BFT-token in red/pink, generally improve scores over Base/SFT/DFT across model sizes and benchmarks, with larger models often scoring higher and approaching or exceeding the GeneAgent reference in some settings.**

vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure comparing gene embedding/model methods.

Panel a: Three 2D scatter/UMAP-style plots labeled `scGPT`, `GenePT`, and `BFT`, showing gene categories as colored points. Legend includes gene biotypes such as protein_coding, lncRNA, miRNA, rRNA, pseudogene, IG_V_gene, TR_V_gene, snoRNA, snRNA, and others. The visible finding is that GenePT and BFT show more separated clusters by gene biotype than scGPT, where points appear more mixed.

Panel b: Bar charts of AUC performance for methods `scGPT`, `GenePT`, and `BFT`. Left chart is `Single gene input` with x-axis tasks including `TF range`, `Dosage sensitivity`, `Biased in male`, `Biased in female`, and `Bivalent in hPAs`. Right chart is `Multi gene input` with tasks `GDA` and `PPI`. BFT generally has the highest or near-highest AUC across several tasks.

Panel c: Bar charts of clustering performance. Left chart is `Clustering performance (phenotype)` with metrics `ARI`, `AMI`, and `ASW`; right chart is `Clustering performance (cell type)` with the same metrics. Methods compared are `PCA`, `scGPT`, `GenePT`, and `BFT`. GenePT/BFT appear stronger than PCA/scGPT on several clustering metrics, especially AMI for cell type.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 5: Comparison of single-cell perturbation response prediction results.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel bar plot comparing model performance across four cell lines: `hepg2`, `rpe1`, `jurkat`, and `k562`. Each panel has y-axis `Score` and x-axis categories `DES`, `PDS`, and `MAE`. Bars are grouped by legend entries `BFT`, `STATE-SE`, and `STATE-small`, with error bars shown.

Main visible finding: `PDS` scores are highest across all panels, generally around 0.6-0.7 with large error bars. `DES` scores are lower, varying by cell line and model, while `MAE` scores are near zero across all cell lines.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 6: Workflow for extracting biological embeddings from LLM-BFT. a : LLM-BFT generates profile texts for entities of interest (e.g., a specific gene). The gene profile text is encoded by OpenAI TEXT-EMBEDDING-ADA-002 (the same text encoder GenePT uses) to obtain gene embeddings, so that GenePT (GPT-4o + ada-002) and LLM-BFT (BFT-70B + ada-002) differ only in the LLM that produces the profile text. b : For a single-cell dataset, gene embeddings are weighted by gene expression values to generate cell embeddings.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture schematic with two labeled panels, **a** and **b**. Panel **a** shows an LLM-based gene text embedding pipeline: a user prompt (“Tell me about gene.”) is processed by **LLM-BFT**, producing an LLM response with gene name/function/interaction text; texts for gene x through gene y are converted via **Text to embedding** into a **gene embedding (N, 2048)** matrix. Panel **b** shows a cell-by-gene expression matrix for **M cells** and **N genes** multiplied by the **gene embedding (N, 2048)** matrix to produce a **cell embedding (M, 2048)** matrix. Main visible message: gene-level text embeddings are derived from LLM responses and combined with gene expression data to generate cell embeddings.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 7: UMAP visualization of the multi-gene input task. a : For GGI, the input embedding of the classifier is directly concatenated from the embeddings of two genes. b : For PPI, the input embedding of the classifier is directly concatenated from the embeddings of two proteins.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel UMAP visualization comparing embeddings from scGPT, GenePT, and BFT. Panels are labeled **a** and **b**.

Panel **a** shows three UMAP scatter plots titled scGPT, GenePT, and BFT, with axes **UMAP1** and **UMAP2**. Points represent gene or protein pairs colored by binary interaction label **0** and **1**. The visible finding is that the models show different degrees of separation between interaction classes, with GenePT and BFT showing more visibly structured class regions than scGPT.

Panel **b** shows three UMAP scatter plots for protein pairs, again comparing scGPT, GenePT, and BFT. Points are colored by interaction type legend: **activation, binding, catalysis, expression, inhibition, ptmod, reaction**. The visible finding is that BFT forms more separated local clusters by interaction category, while scGPT and GenePT appear more centrally mixed.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 8: UMAP visualization of cell-level embeddings. a : PCA embeddings of the raw data, colored by cell type labels (cell type heterogeneity), patient labels (batch labels), and phenotype labels (disease heterogeneity), respectively. b : Cell embeddings derived from LLM-BFT, colored by cell type labels (cell type heterogeneity), patient labels (batch labels), and phenotype labels (disease heterogeneity), respectively.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel UMAP scatter plot figure with two labeled rows/panels, **a** and **b**. Each row contains three UMAP plots with axes **UMAP1** and **UMAP2**, colored by **celltype**, **patient**, and **phenotype**.

Legends show cell types including BCell, EC, Fibroblast, MSC, Mastcell, MonoMaphDC, NK, Plasma, SMC1, SMC2, Tcell, and Unknown; patient IDs including affected and control samples; and phenotypes including **Ascending only**, **Ascending to descending**, **Ascending w/ root**, and **Control**.

The figure shows single-cell clustering structure and annotation across patients and phenotypes. Visibly, panel **a** has more separated clusters, while panel **b** shows broader, more continuous/overlapping UMAP distributions. Phenotype coloring indicates disease/control groups occupy partly distinct but overlapping regions across the embeddings.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 9: UMAP visualization of single-cell multimodal data integration results. Rows 1 to 4 represent different integration methods, respectively. Columns 1 to 3 correspond to different coloring labels (modality, cell type, and donor), respectively.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel UMAP embedding comparison figure from a single-cell multi-omics integration experiment. The grid has 4 rows labeled `BFT`, `BBKNN`, `Harmony`, and `scMODAL`, and 3 columns colored by `modality`, `celltype`, and `donor`.

Each panel shows a 2D UMAP plot with axes `UMAP1` and `UMAP2`. Legends indicate modality labels `ADT` and `RNA`; cell types including `B`, `CD4 T`, `CD8 T`, `DC`, `Mono`, `NK`, `other`, and `other T`; and donors `P1` through `P8`.

The figure compares how different integration methods mix modalities and donors while preserving cell-type structure. Visibly, `scMODAL` and `BFT` show stronger overlap between ADT and RNA modalities than `BBKNN` or `Harmony`, while cell-type clusters remain distinguishable across methods.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: (a) Embeddings (E) from Biological Foundation Models (BioFMs) are input to Bio-BLIP to provide multiple modalities of information, here from AlphaGenome , GenePT , and ESM-2 . (b) Modality-specific Q-formers align diverse biological embeddings with captions of genomic variants, which contain functional and locational information. The Q-formers output query tokens encoding relevant information from each modality. (c) The Master Qformer integrates modality-specific tokens through cross-attention, producing a fixed-length visual prefix (d) The LLM, its weights frozen , takes as input the multimodal prefix and a prompt. During pretraining, the LLM loss backpropagates only to train the Q-formers. Pretraining and evaluation is conducted on variant annotation; all weights are frozen and the model is then applied to downstream evaluation tasks.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Model architecture/workflow diagram labeled “BioBLIP Architecture.” It shows panel-like labels A-D: A indicates multiple input embedding sources (AlphaGenome Ref/Alt embeddings, GenoPT embeddings, ESM Protein embeddings) as blue triangular inputs E1, E2, … En; B shows modality-specific query modules (“DNA Qformer,” “Gene Qformer,” “Protein Qformer”) producing DNA/gene/protein-specific query tokens; C shows a “Master Qformer” receiving query tokens plus an instruction describing genomic variant context and outputting a fixed-length variant prefix; D shows this prefix fed with a text prompt into a “Frozen LLM,” producing a generated variant annotation JSON.

No quantitative axes or plots are present. The biological/model content shown is a multimodal genomic variant annotation architecture integrating DNA, gene, and protein embeddings for tasks including variant annotation, target gene identification, and regulatory variant prioritization. Main visible finding/claim: BioBLIP uses chained Q-former modules to convert heterogeneous biological embeddings into an LLM-compatible prefix for structured variant annotation.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Radar/spider plot comparing four genomic annotation resources across four axes: Variant Type, Chromosome Location, Nearest Genes, and Variant Consequence. The radial scale is labeled 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%. Legend shows AFG, ESM, GENE, and BioLIP Stage 2.

BioLIP Stage 2 appears as a dashed outline reaching 100% on all four axes. Among the other datasets, GENE has high coverage for chromosome location and nearest genes, AFG is high for variant type and variant consequence but very low for nearest genes, and ESM is intermediate overall.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 3: Target Gene Identification . (Left) Accuracy on all reasoning traces. (Right) Accuracy on reasoning traces where the target gene is not the closest gene.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Two-panel bar chart comparing gene trace performance across language/model systems. Left panel is titled “All Gene Traces (n = 396)” with percentage y-axis and bars for Baseline - Closest Gene, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-32B, Bio-BLIP (Ours), and Claude Sonnet 4.6. Values shown are 56.3%, 59.6%, 64.4%, 71.2%, and 75.8%, with Bio-BLIP highlighted in purple and annotated as +6.8 percentage points over Qwen3-32B.

Right panel is titled “Non-closest Gene Traces (n = 175)” with the same model labels and percentage y-axis. Values shown are 0%, 19.4%, 29.7%, 41.1%, and 46.3%, with Bio-BLIP highlighted and annotated as +11.4 percentage points over Qwen3-32B.

Main visible finding: Bio-BLIP outperforms Qwen3-32B on both all gene traces and non-closest gene traces, while Claude Sonnet 4.6 has the highest displayed percentages overall.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

A horizontal dot-and-line accuracy plot comparing several models on “Accuracy (10 options).” The x-axis runs from 0% to 100%, with model names on the y-axis: Random, Qwen3-32B, Evo2-7B, GPN Promoter, Bio-BLIP (Ours), and GPN MSA. Each row shows Top-1 accuracy and Top-2 accuracy as dark points connected by a line, with a legend at lower right.

Visible values include Random 10.0%/20.0%, Qwen3-32B 19.8%/28.7%, Evo2-7B 37.3%/47.6%, GPN Promoter 38.8%/51.2%, Bio-BLIP 48.2%/53.0%, and GPN MSA 68.9%/80.2%. The main finding is that GPN MSA has the highest Top-1 and Top-2 accuracy, while Bio-BLIP (Ours) outperforms the other non-GPN-MSA baselines shown.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Two-panel experimental results figure showing BioBLIP validation performance and ablation.

Top panel: line plot titled “Validation Set Performance vs Training Epoch.” X-axis is Epoch, y-axis is Mean JSON Accuracy. Legend compares BioBLIP in blue vs “BioBLIP - No Master Model” in orange. BioBLIP accuracy increases steadily from about 32% to about 52%, while the no-master-model variant fluctuates around 26–38% and plateaus near 35%.

Bottom panel: grouped bar chart titled “Master Model Ablation.” Y-axis is Score, with categories Nearest Genes (Exact Match), Chromosome, Consequence, Cell Type (ROUGE), and Variant Type. Legend again compares BioBLIP vs BioBLIP - No Master Model. BioBLIP outperforms the ablated model in all categories, with annotated gains of approximately +35.0 pp, +17.8 pp, +1.3 pp, +1.0 pp, and +0.8 pp respectively.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 6: Stage 1 Evaluation Losses for Bio-BLIP with Embeddings permuted to incorrect variants (blue), versus Embeddings matched with the correct variants (orange).
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Three-panel line plot showing training loss over steps for two runs, with a legend indicating blue = `Ablated Embedding` and orange = `Embedding`.

Panels are labeled `itc_sum`, `itm_sum`, and `itg_sum`. Each panel has x-axis `Step` and y-axis `Loss`.

Main visible findings:
- `itc_sum`: Ablated Embedding loss stays high and slightly increases, while Embedding loss steadily decreases.
- `itm_sum`: Both runs fluctuate substantially; Embedding dips sharply around step 7 and spikes near step 11.
- `itg_sum`: Both losses decrease over steps, with Ablated Embedding consistently lower than Embedding after the first steps.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: Overview of our pretraining framework, ALTER . (a) ALTER processes each modality using modality-specific encoders, followed by a universal sequence Transformer and task-specific projection heads for downstream prediction. (b) The three-tiered constraints of ALTER, which can enable model to align multimodal inputs without requiring full modality pairing. (c) ALTER can be applied to any downstream task by integrating task-specific projection heads for fine-tuning.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel model architecture/workflow figure for a biomedical multi-modal foundation model. Panel (a) “Overall Architecture” shows inputs from whole slide images, omics, and pathology reports processed by modality-specific tokenizers/encoders, sequence projectors, a Universal Sequence Transformer, and task-specific projection heads. Panel (b) “Stage 1: Pre-training Universal Sequence Transformer” shows contrastive and masked language modeling objectives across WSI, omics, and text features, including inter-modal, inter-sample, and intra-modal contrast. Panel (c) “Stage 2: Training Task Projection Heads with Downstream Tasks” shows downstream applications including cancer subtyping, survival analysis, and report generation. No quantitative axes or experimental results are shown; the main content is a proposed multimodal training pipeline/architecture.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 2: Universal sequence Transformer architecture of ALTER.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Model architecture diagram showing a modular neural network block. The figure contains labeled components: “Modality-Specific Decoupling” with three branches “Slide MLP,” “Omics MLP,” and “Report MLP,” followed by a summation/addition node, then “Modality-Shared Fusion” containing “Modality Shared MSA.” Arrows indicate information flow upward through the shared fusion module into modality-specific branches, with residual/skip-style connections along the right side. No axes, numeric data, legend, or biological measurements are shown. The main content is a multimodal fusion architecture separating modality-specific processing from shared attention/fusion.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 3: ALTER's overall performance across all datasets. The base model denotes commonly used task-specific benchmarks (marked with † in § 4.2), while the suboptimal model refers to the model with the second-best overall performance for the specific task type.

Radar/spider plot comparing three model variants across biomedical benchmark datasets/tasks. The legend shows Base Model in green, Suboptimal Model in blue, and ALTER in purple. Dataset/task labels around the plot include UCEC, STAD, KIRP, KIRC, BRACS, PANDA, TUPAC-16, UBC-OCEAN, TP53, EGFR, and PatchGastricADC22.

ALTER generally forms the outermost polygon, indicating the strongest overall performance across most tasks. figure_candidates.caption: Figure 4: Analysis of the performance of ALTER. For cancer subtyping, a unimodal task, we freeze the fusion blocks to prevent multimodal information from being corrupted; for survival prediction as a multimodal task, we unfreeze them, where PT stands for pretraining, and FL stands for fusion layer.

Grouped bar-chart figure with two panels: (a) “Cancer subtyping” and (b) “Survival prediction.” Each panel compares four methods in the legend: PT-WSI, PT-OMIC, FL-Frozen, and FL-Unfrozen.

Panel (a) shows cancer subtyping performance across BRACS, PANDA, TUPAC-16, and UBC-OCEAN, with y-axis values roughly from 0.40 to 1.00. FL-based methods, especially FL-Unfrozen, appear highest for UBC-OCEAN and competitive across datasets.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: (a) Embeddings (E) from Biological Foundation Models (BioFMs) are input to Bio-BLIP to provide multiple modalities of information, here from AlphaGenome , GenePT , and ESM-2 . (b) Modality-specific Q-formers align diverse biological embeddings with captions of genomic variants, which contain functional and locational information. The Q-formers output query tokens encoding relevant information from each modality. (c) The Master Qformer integrates modality-specific tokens through cross-attention, producing a fixed-length visual prefix (d) The LLM, its weights frozen , takes as input the multimodal prefix and a prompt. During pretraining, the LLM loss backpropagates only to train the Q-formers. Pretraining and evaluation is conducted on variant annotation; all weights are frozen and the model is then applied to downstream evaluation tasks.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Model architecture/workflow diagram labeled “BioBLIP Architecture.” It shows panel-like labels A-D: A indicates multiple input embedding sources (AlphaGenome Ref/Alt embeddings, GenoPT embeddings, ESM Protein embeddings) as blue triangular inputs E1, E2, … En; B shows modality-specific query modules (“DNA Qformer,” “Gene Qformer,” “Protein Qformer”) producing DNA/gene/protein-specific query tokens; C shows a “Master Qformer” receiving query tokens plus an instruction describing genomic variant context and outputting a fixed-length variant prefix; D shows this prefix fed with a text prompt into a “Frozen LLM,” producing a generated variant annotation JSON.

No quantitative axes or plots are present. The biological/model content shown is a multimodal genomic variant annotation architecture integrating DNA, gene, and protein embeddings for tasks including variant annotation, target gene identification, and regulatory variant prioritization. Main visible finding/claim: BioBLIP uses chained Q-former modules to convert heterogeneous biological embeddings into an LLM-compatible prefix for structured variant annotation.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Radar/spider plot comparing four genomic annotation resources across four axes: Variant Type, Chromosome Location, Nearest Genes, and Variant Consequence. The radial scale is labeled 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%. Legend shows AFG, ESM, GENE, and BioLIP Stage 2.

BioLIP Stage 2 appears as a dashed outline reaching 100% on all four axes. Among the other datasets, GENE has high coverage for chromosome location and nearest genes, AFG is high for variant type and variant consequence but very low for nearest genes, and ESM is intermediate overall.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 3: Target Gene Identification . (Left) Accuracy on all reasoning traces. (Right) Accuracy on reasoning traces where the target gene is not the closest gene.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Two-panel bar chart comparing gene trace performance across language/model systems. Left panel is titled “All Gene Traces (n = 396)” with percentage y-axis and bars for Baseline - Closest Gene, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-32B, Bio-BLIP (Ours), and Claude Sonnet 4.6. Values shown are 56.3%, 59.6%, 64.4%, 71.2%, and 75.8%, with Bio-BLIP highlighted in purple and annotated as +6.8 percentage points over Qwen3-32B.

Right panel is titled “Non-closest Gene Traces (n = 175)” with the same model labels and percentage y-axis. Values shown are 0%, 19.4%, 29.7%, 41.1%, and 46.3%, with Bio-BLIP highlighted and annotated as +11.4 percentage points over Qwen3-32B.

Main visible finding: Bio-BLIP outperforms Qwen3-32B on both all gene traces and non-closest gene traces, while Claude Sonnet 4.6 has the highest displayed percentages overall.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

A horizontal dot-and-line accuracy plot comparing several models on “Accuracy (10 options).” The x-axis runs from 0% to 100%, with model names on the y-axis: Random, Qwen3-32B, Evo2-7B, GPN Promoter, Bio-BLIP (Ours), and GPN MSA. Each row shows Top-1 accuracy and Top-2 accuracy as dark points connected by a line, with a legend at lower right.

Visible values include Random 10.0%/20.0%, Qwen3-32B 19.8%/28.7%, Evo2-7B 37.3%/47.6%, GPN Promoter 38.8%/51.2%, Bio-BLIP 48.2%/53.0%, and GPN MSA 68.9%/80.2%. The main finding is that GPN MSA has the highest Top-1 and Top-2 accuracy, while Bio-BLIP (Ours) outperforms the other non-GPN-MSA baselines shown.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Two-panel experimental results figure showing BioBLIP validation performance and ablation.

Top panel: line plot titled “Validation Set Performance vs Training Epoch.” X-axis is Epoch, y-axis is Mean JSON Accuracy. Legend compares BioBLIP in blue vs “BioBLIP - No Master Model” in orange. BioBLIP accuracy increases steadily from about 32% to about 52%, while the no-master-model variant fluctuates around 26–38% and plateaus near 35%.

Bottom panel: grouped bar chart titled “Master Model Ablation.” Y-axis is Score, with categories Nearest Genes (Exact Match), Chromosome, Consequence, Cell Type (ROUGE), and Variant Type. Legend again compares BioBLIP vs BioBLIP - No Master Model. BioBLIP outperforms the ablated model in all categories, with annotated gains of approximately +35.0 pp, +17.8 pp, +1.3 pp, +1.0 pp, and +0.8 pp respectively.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: The architecture of BioMedGPT.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Conceptual workflow/model architecture diagram for **BioMedGPT**. It shows two input domains at the top: **“Language of Life”** with molecule, protein, and cell examples, and **“Natural Language”** with knowledge graph, text, and experiment examples. These feed into a **Multimodal Encoder**, then **Neural Alignment and Translation**, then **BioMedGPT-LM**, producing a reasoning-enabled **BioMedGPT** system.

No axes or quantitative data are shown. The figure illustrates the model pipeline: biological modalities are “deciphered,” natural-language resources are “empowered,” both are aligned through a multimodal encoder and language model, and free-text user inquiries are transformed into scientific insights through thinking and reasoning.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 2: The overview of BioMedGPT-10B. BioMedGPT-LM is the large language model of BioMedGPT, which serves as a cognitive core to jointly comprehend various biological modalities through natural language. In BioMedGPT-10B, the parameter size of the large language model is 7B. BioMedGPT-10B adopts GraphMVP [Liu et al., 2022] as the 2D molecular graph encoder, ESM2-3B [Lin et al., 2022] as the protein sequence encoder, and conducts feature space alignment via a neural network adaptor. BioMedGPT can be applied to many multimodal downstream tasks such as biomedical QA, molecule QA, and protein QA.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: BIOREASON Architecture. Schematic representation of our novel multimodal framework that integrates a DNA foundation model with a Large Language Model.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture diagram for a genomics-language model system. It shows DNA sequences passed through a frozen Evo2-1B model, then a learnable linear projection aligning Evo2 embeddings to Qwen3 dimensions. These projected DNA embeddings are stacked with tokenized text embeddings from a BioReason chat template and Qwen3 tokenizer, using special DNA pad/start/end tokens and a Qwen3 embedding matrix. The combined embeddings feed into a Qwen3-4B model.

Visible labels include “Stacked DNA and Text Embeddings,” “Frozen Evo2-1B,” “Learnable Linear Projection,” “Qwen3 Tokenizer,” “Qwen3 Embedding Matrix,” “BioReason Chat Template,” “Question,” and “Response (with reasoning).” The example biomedical prompt concerns chromosome 12, pathway definition involving LRRK2, CYCS, APAF1, CASP9, and CASP3, and asks about the biological effect of an LRRK2 allele. The response panel gives chain-of-thought-style tags and concludes “Parkinson’s disease.”

Main visible point: the figure illustrates a multimodal architecture combining DNA sequence embeddings with biomedical text prompts to generate disease-related reasoning responses.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 2: BIOREASON Dataset Curation and Composition. A. Representative example of a KEGG Variant Network element from the 298 networks utilized in our study, illustrating the relationship between genomic variants and their corresponding disease annotation that serves as ground truth for generating mechanistic reasoning traces. B. Exemplar of a structured question-answer pair with an accompanying multi-step reasoning trace demonstrating the expected logical progression from genomic variant to phenotypic outcome. C. Pipeline for data acquisition, integration, and curation across the three BIOREASON tasks. D. Distribution of train/test splits across the three curated datasets. 10% of train dataset was used for validation. E. Distribution of disease categories represented within the datasets, highlighting the diversity of variants and diseases represented in the datasets.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific workflow and dataset summary figure for a biomedical question-answering/reasoning dataset built from KEGG variant networks and disease annotations.

Panels:
- **A**: Schematic of a KEGG variant network-to-disease example. Shows pathway, gene names, associated disease, and a ground-truth literature statement. Example involves **LRRK2**, pathway **LRRK2 -> CYCS -> APAF1 -> CASP9 -> CASP3**, and **Parkinson’s Disease**.
- **B**: Example question-answer pair and reasoning trace. The question includes a variant sequence and chromosome number, network definition, genes, and asks for the biological effect/disease. The reasoning trace identifies a **C-to-G substitution**, links it to an LRRK2 gain-of-function mutation, and concludes **Parkinson’s Disease**.
- **C**: Workflow diagram showing three task pipelines: KEGG pathway, coding variants, and coding non-SNVs. Data sources include KEGG, ClinVar, dbSNP, OMIM, COSMIC, and GPT-4o formatting. Outputs include **1,449 QA pairs**, **60,810 QA pairs**, and **36,088 QA pairs**.
- **D**: Stacked bar chart showing train/validation/test split percentages for KEGG, Task 2, and Task 3 QA pairs. Most data are train/validation, with smaller test sets labeled **290**, **1,233**, and **873**.
- **E**: Stacked bar chart showing disease-category composition across KEGG, Task 2, and Task 3. Legend includes benign, cardiovascular, immunological, metabolic, musculoskeletal, neurological, oncological, other, and sensory disorder categories.

Main visible finding: the figure presents construction of a variant-network biomedical reasoning QA benchmark, with thousands of generated QA pairs spanning multiple variant tasks and disease categories.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: BIOVERSE base architecture: a modality-specific BioFM encodes a biological entity, and its output embeddings are mapped by a projection layer into the LLM's embedding space via special tokens (e.g. [BIO] ). In the alignment stage, only the projection layer P θ is trainable, while the encoder f b and the LLM g remain frozen. In the subsequent instruction-tuning stage, we allow both P θ and the low-rank adapter (LORA) within the LLM to be trainable. Stage 1 (S1) can be trained using autoregressive (AR) or contrastive (CT) loss, while stage 2 (S2) is always AR.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Figure type: workflow/model architecture diagram for a biomedical machine learning method integrating scRNA-seq data and text prompts/labels.

Visible panels/labels: Inputs on the left include “scRNA-seq Data” with a heatmap-like expression matrix labeled row = cell, column = gene, color = expression value, plus “Text (Prompt)” and “Text (Label)” examples. The center shows BioEncoder, LLM Tokenizer, LLM Embedding Layer, CLS/X-pooling, projection layers, and a 2-layer MLP. The right side shows a LoRA module and “LLM Forward Pass,” with training paths labeled S1 and S2. Colored annotations indicate BIO token injection, CT training, and AR auto-regressive training.

Quantity/process shown: It depicts how cell embeddings from scRNA-seq are projected into the LLM token space and injected as soft tokens alongside prompt embeddings, then used to predict label tokens such as a cell type.

Main visible finding/message: The diagram presents a model pipeline for cell-type prediction or annotation using scRNA-seq-derived embeddings combined with LLM prompt/label token embeddings, with optional LoRA fine-tuning and auto-regressive training.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 2: UMAP visualization of scRNA-seq and text embeddings. Left: before alignment, cell embeddings (green) form isolated clusters within the LLM embedding space. Right: after alignment, cell embeddings are pulled closer to biologically relevant text and separated from unrelated generaldomain text. BIOVERSE successfully realigns the modalities into a shared representation space.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: C2S-Scale unifies transcriptomics and natural language for scalable single-cell analysis. A , The C2S-Scale corpus integrates over 50 million single-cell transcriptomes curated from the CELLxGENE and Human Cell Atlas repositories, linking transcriptomic profiles with rich cell, tissue, and donor-level metadata as well as scientific abstracts and papers. B , C2S-Scale expands upon the Cell2Sentence framework by increasing model capacity up to 27 billion parameters, building a multi-task training corpus of over 1 trillion tokens, and expanding task diversity to include multimodal and multicellular inputs. C , Transcriptomic profiles are transformed into 'cell sentences', ordered sequences of gene names ranked by expression level. This enables the direct application of pretrained LLMs without requiring architectural modifications. D , C2S-Scale is initialized from pre-trained LLM checkpoints. An initial training phase on cell sentences is followed by instruction fine-tuning for a variety of downstream tasks. E , This unified training regime enables broad downstream capabilities, ranging from standard cell annotation to complex tasks like perturbation prediction and biological question answering.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel schematic overview figure for a biomedical AI model/workflow, likely a cell-language foundation model.

Figure type: conceptual workflow/model architecture diagram with labeled panels A-E.

Visible panels and labels:
- A. Data Sources and Annotations: icons for single-cell data, cell clusters, tissue sections, paper abstracts, and donor metadata. Reported scale includes 800+ datasets, 170M+ single-cell and bulk samples, 100M+ annotations, 21M+ perturbations, and 1B+ tokens.
- B. Scaling Dimensions: four boxed concepts: Model Capacity, Dataset Size, Multimodality, and Context Diversity.
- C. Cell Sentence Representation: converts a gene expression matrix with cells and genes into “cell sentences” listing gene tokens.
- D. Model Training Procedure: three-stage training flow: natural language pre-training with a base LLM, continued training on cell sentences to create C2S-Scale, then instruction fine-tuning for downstream tasks.
- E. Downstream Tasks: examples include cell type annotation, cell generation, perturbation response prediction, cluster captioning, dataset interpretation, and question answering.

Biological/model quantity shown: scale and modality of single-cell datasets, gene-expression-derived token sequences, and model training/use cases.

Main visible finding/message: the figure presents a unified framework for training a language-model-based system on large-scale single-cell, perturbation, metadata, and text resources, enabling multiple downstream biological interpretation and generation tasks.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 2: Caption continued on following page.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel benchmark figure with quantitative results for single-cell foundation/model methods.

Panel A shows a matrix of task performance scores across models, including C2S, scGPT, Geneformer, scFoundation, Gemini-1.5, GPT-4o, linear classifier, PCA, scVI, and CellTypist. Columns include cell type annotation tasks, cell embedding tasks, and generative tasks. Blue circles encode performance from 0 to 1, yellow outlines mark best performers, and gray dots indicate incapable/N/A. Bar summaries on the right aggregate predictive, generative, and overall scores.

Panel B shows compute scaling laws as bubble plots with x-axis training compute in log10 PetaFLOP days and y-axis BERTScore or gene overlap metrics. Bubble size denotes model scale, and colors distinguish tasks.

Panel C shows out-of-distribution cell type annotation accuracy versus training compute, comparing foundation models and simpler baselines, with bubble size indicating parameter count and shading/legend distinguishing model type.

Panel D shows LoRA fine-tuning performance for 27B and 2B base models, plotting training compute versus cell type BERTScore and dataset interpretation BERTScore for different ranks.

Panel E shows sample efficiency scaling with training samples seen on the x-axis and BERTScore or expressed gene overlap on the y-axes.

Main visible finding: the C2S models, especially larger versions, achieve top or near-top performance across predictive, embedding, generative, OOD, compute-scaling, and sample-efficiency evaluations compared with other single-cell models and baselines.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 3: C2S-Scale enables natural language interpretation across biological hierarchies, from single cells to entire datasets. A , Overview of different scales of biological data interpretation, from single cells to cluster and datasetlevel annotation. B , Single-cell annotation performance on a diverse immune cell atlas [21]. The correspondence between ground truth and predicted labels demonstrates accurate annotation at the single-cell level. C , Cell annotation performance of C2S-Scale versus foundation model and simple model baselines in an in-distribution versus out-ofdistribution setting. C2S-Scale exhibits the smallest performance degradation when transferring from in-distribution (ID) to out-of-distribution (OOD) immune cell contexts. D , Cluster captioning performance on unseen data clusters. Models are tasked with generating descriptive biological captions given multi-cell context, with quality measured by BioBERTScore. E-F , Dataset-level summarization performance. Models generate natural language abstracts for entire scRNA-seq experiments, evaluated on held-out cells from seen studies (E) and completely unseen studies (F). Error bars represent standard deviation across test set samples.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing evaluation of a model for single-cell / spatial biological interpretation.

Panels:
- **A**: Workflow schematic titled “Multi-scale biological interpretation.” UMAP-style embeddings are shown at three levels: **Single Cell**, **Cell Cluster**, and **Dataset / Tissue**, with example user-model dialogue boxes for cell type identification, cluster description, and dataset summary.
- **B**: Confusion matrix heatmap comparing **True Cell Types** vs **Predicted Cell Types**, with a prediction accuracy color scale from 0 to 1.
- **C**: Bar chart titled **ID vs OOD Evaluation Setup**, comparing model accuracy across methods under **In-distribution (ID)** and **Out-of-distribution (OOD)** settings. Methods include C2S-Scale-28M, scGPT, Geneformer, scFoundation, scVI, PCA, CellTypist, and Linear classifier. C2S-Scale-28M appears highest or among the highest in both ID and OOD.
- **D**: Bar chart for **Cluster Captioning**, y-axis labeled **BERTScore**, comparing multiple models. C2S-Scale-27B appears best among shown methods.
- **E**: Bar chart for **Dataset Interpretation (ID)** with y-axis **BERTScore**, comparing models; C2S-Scale variants, especially larger ones, score highest.
- **F**: Bar chart for **Dataset Interpretation (OOD)** with y-axis **BERTScore**, again showing C2S-Scale models among the strongest performers.

Main visible finding: C2S-Scale models appear to outperform or match competing single-cell foundation/model baselines across cell type prediction, cluster captioning, and dataset interpretation, including out-of-distribution evaluation.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 4: C2S-Scale can interpret multi-cellular spatial context and predict niche neighborhoods. A, We fine-tune C2S-Scale on a variety of single and multi-cellular spatial tasks designed to enable C2S-Scale to perform spatial reasoning, including identifying whether cells belong to the same neighborhood, generating spatial neighbors, and predicting the niche label of a cell or group of cells. A 'neighborhood' is defined to be cells within a fixed radius from a central cell. B, C2S outperforms Nicheformer, scGPT, and other models in spatial neighborhood prediction accuracy (* = P < 0.05, ** = P < 0.01; McNemar's test). Dashed line represents random baseline accuracy (0.51). C, We use publicly available gene interaction databases including BioGRID and CellPhoneDB to construct natural language interaction prompts about gene interactions. Integrating gene interactions from BioGRID and CellPhoneDB individually improves performance, and their combination provides the greatest improvement (Panel B). These results highlight the multi-task transfer learning potential of C2S-Scale for spatially-aware biological modeling.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure combining a workflow schematic, benchmark plot, and optimization diagram.

Panel A shows a biomedical question-answering example for single-cell RNA-seq interpretation. It includes a context about inhibitory neurons in the thalamus, a “scRNA-seq Data” cell sentence with gene names, a question asking whether the cell is an inhibitory neuron, and an answer citing GAD1 and GAD2 as evidence for GABA synthesis and inhibitory neuron identity.

Panel B is a bar plot with y-axis labeled “BioBERT Score” ranging roughly from 0.65 to 0.85. A delta sentence captures the vector difference between a perturbed and control state ( ∆ E = E stimulated -E control). figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: C2S-Scale unifies transcriptomics and natural language for scalable single-cell analysis. A , The C2S-Scale corpus integrates over 50 million single-cell transcriptomes curated from the CELLxGENE and Human Cell Atlas repositories, linking transcriptomic profiles with rich cell, tissue, and donor-level metadata as well as scientific abstracts and papers. B , C2S-Scale expands upon the Cell2Sentence framework by increasing model capacity up to 27 billion parameters, building a multi-task training corpus of over 1 trillion tokens, and expanding task diversity to include multimodal and multicellular inputs. C , Transcriptomic profiles are transformed into 'cell sentences', ordered sequences of gene names ranked by expression level. This enables the direct application of pretrained LLMs without requiring architectural modifications. D , C2S-Scale is initialized from pre-trained LLM checkpoints. An initial training phase on cell sentences is followed by instruction fine-tuning for a variety of downstream tasks. E , This unified training regime enables broad downstream capabilities, ranging from standard cell annotation to complex tasks like perturbation prediction and biological question answering.

B, C2S outperforms Nicheformer, scGPT, and other models in spatial neighborhood prediction accuracy (* = P < 0.05, ** = P < 0.01; McNemar's test). These results highlight the multi-task transfer learning potential of C2S-Scale for spatially-aware biological modeling.

- Panel C: cytokine stimulation benchmark bar plots for scFID, MMD, and Wasserstein-2 distance, comparing C2S-scale 410M, C2S-scale 1B, scGen, CellOT, scGPT, ConDor, BioLord, and linear models.
- Panel D: cytokine stimulation response plots for IFN response and IL1000 apoptosis response, showing scFID, Kendall tau, and Pearson r for SFT vs GRPO at 410M and 1B model scales.
- Panel E: SciPlex benchmark bar plots for scFID, MMD, and Wasserstein-1, comparing C2S-scale 410M/1B against scGPT, chemCPA, and ConDor.

Main visible finding: C2S-scale models, especially the 1B version, show lower distributional error metrics than comparison methods in several benchmarks, while reinforcement learning/GRPO appears to improve correlation metrics over SFT in panel D.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 7: Virtual screening with C2S-Scale nominates a context-dependent modulator of antigen presentation. A, Schematic of the dual-context virtual screening workflow. The model predicts perturbation outcomes on MHC-I antigen presentation gene sets using initial states derived from primary tumor profiles (immune context-positive) and cell line profiles (immune context-neutral). B, Volcano plot displaying predicted drug effects in the primary tumor screen. Silmitasertib (red star) is identified as a high-scoring novel candidate. Inset details the top-ranking compounds, stratified by prior evidence: known MHC-I modulators (dark blue), plausible candidates with pathway links (light blue), and novel hits (grey). C, Experimental validation of the positive control, trametinib. Dose-response assessment of HLA-A,B,C surface levels (Mean Fluorescence Intensity; MFI) in WAGA cells treated with indicated concentrations of trametinib in the absence (gray) or presence (blue) of IFNβ (2 U/ml). D, Predicted context specificity of silmitasertib, showing a significantly higher antigen presentation score in the primary tumor context compared to the cell line context. E, Experimental validation of the novel hit, silmitasertib. Dose-response assessment of MHC-I MFI (normalized to vehicle control) in WAGA cells treated with silmitasertib without (gray) or with (blue) low-dose IFNβ (2 U/ml). Error bars represent mean ± s.d. Significance calculated via two-way t-test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons; ∗ P < 0 . 05 , ∗ ∗ P < 0 . 01 , ∗ ∗ ∗ P < 0 . 001 , ∗ ∗ ∗ ∗ P < 0 . 0001 .

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel biomedical experimental figure showing a virtual drug-screening workflow and validation results.

Panel A is a schematic workflow labeled “Virtual Screening Workflow”: primary tumors with immune context-positive profiles and immune-neutral cell lines are screened against a compound library of 4000+ drugs using C2S, identifying hits that increase MHC-I antigen presentation gene set score versus compounds with no effect.

Panel B is a volcano/scatter plot titled “Primary Tumor Screen Results,” with x-axis “Predicted Antigen Presentation Score” and y-axis “-log10(p-value).” Points are categorized by legend as Reported, Plausible, Novel, and star-marked “Silmitasertib.” A zoomed inset highlights drugs including crizotinib, nutlin-3, GSK-126, trametinib, afatinib, paclitaxel, and silmitasertib, with “16 / 23 Reported or Plausible.”

Panel C is a bar plot for “Trametinib + IFNβ (Known Hit - Positive Control)” measuring “HLA ABC MFI” across trametinib concentrations in nM, comparing DMSO only versus DMSO + 5 U/ml IFNβ. HLA ABC MFI increases with treatment, especially with IFNβ.

Panel D is a bar plot titled “Silmitasertib Context Specificity,” showing predicted antigen presentation score higher in “Primary Tumor Context” than “WAGA Cell Line Context,” marked significant.

Panel E is a bar plot for “Silmitasertib + IFNβ (Novel Hit - C2S-predicted)” measuring “HLA ABC MFI” across silmitasertib concentrations in nM, comparing DMSO only versus DMSO + 2 U/ml IFNβ. The main visible finding is that silmitasertib with IFNβ strongly increases HLA ABC MFI relative to DMSO-only conditions.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the CaLMFlow framework. CaLMFlow takes as input textual conditions and flows and generates the next time point for the flows. The textual condition is tokenized and embedded using the LLM tokenizer and embedding layer while the conditional flows are transformed into spatial-temporal tokens using a learned projection. If multiple conditional flows are input simultaneously, the tokens are ordered by flow, space, and then time. The LLM applies causal language modeling and generates the next time point for each flow.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture schematic for generating conditional single-cell flows. The figure has four main panels labeled “Input Conditional Flows,” “Tokenized Flow Tensor,” “Next Token Prediction,” and “Generated Flows.” It shows source distributions at `t=0` conditioned on text labels such as cell type and image labels, mapped into a tokenized tensor over time/flow, cell state, and trajectories. The sequentialized tokens are passed to an LLM for next-token prediction using a Volterra integral equation formulation, then decoded with a VAE decoder to produce generated flow distributions at times `t=0`, `t=0.1`, `t=0.2`, …, `t=1`. The main visible idea is a conditional generative pipeline that learns and extrapolates temporal flow trajectories from multimodal conditions.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 2: Heatmaps of the ground truth 4 Gaussians dataset (2a) and that generated by CFM (2b), CaLMFlow (1 traj.) (2c), and CaLMFlow (8 traj.) (2d). Both variants of CaLMFlow generate a distribution that closely matches the ground truth, with the 8-trajectory version further enhancing performance by distributing the data more evenly and accurately.

Multi-panel experiment/result visualization showing four square heatmap/scatter-density images with captions: (a) Ground Truth, (b) CFM, (c) CaLMFlow (1 traj.), and (d) CaLMFlow (8 traj.). There are no visible axes, scale bars, colorbar, or legend. The panels compare spatial point/density distributions: ground truth shows four compact clusters near the image corners; CFM shows a diffuse central cloud with no clear corner structure; CaLMFlow with 1 trajectory partially recovers several clustered regions but remains noisy/diffuse; CaLMFlow with 8 trajectories most closely matches the ground truth with compact clusters near the corners.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 3: Comparison of conditional generation quality across different models for single-cell perturbation data. CaLMFlow (3a and 3b) exhibits strong overlap between generated data distribution (blue) and the ground-truth distribution (orange), highlighting its superior capability to model data with unseen combinatorial perturbations. In contrast, other models struggle to produce realistic samples. For CaLMFlow, R.I. refers to randomly initialized CLM, and N.L. refers to natural language pretrained CLM.

The figure contains eight scatterplot panels labeled (a) CaLMFlow (R.I.), (b) CaLMFlow (N.L.), (c) CFM, (d) CFM-OT, (e) CFM-SB, (f) scVI, (g) scGPT, and (h) CPA. A legend in panel (a) marks blue points as “Generated” and orange points as “Original.” Axes are visible as plot frames but have no tick labels or axis titles.

The figure appears to evaluate how well different generative or transformation models reproduce an original biomedical data distribution, likely single-cell latent/embedding structure. Main visible finding: CaLMFlow panels show stronger overlap between generated and original point clouds, while several other methods show separated clusters, distorted trajectories, or poor alignment between generated and original distributions.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 4: Ablation results on temperature. Left : CaLMFlow generated data from 8gaussians to 2moons, using different temperature values. Right : 2-Wasserstein and MMD performances as a function of temperature. The plots show that a low, non-zero temperature value ( τ =0.2) produces the best performance and that the VAE is necessary.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing simulated 2D distributions and quantitative transport metrics. Left panels: scatter plots labeled “Ground Truth,” “No VAE,” and time points `t=0`, `t=0.2`, `t=1`, `t=2`. Red points are labeled `source` and blue points `target`; ground truth shows spiral-like target structure with separated red source clusters. Subsequent panels show generated/interpolated point clouds becoming more diffuse over time.

Right panel: line plot versus `Temperature (τ)` on the x-axis. Left y-axis is red, labeled `2-Wasserstein`; right y-axis is blue, labeled `MMD`. Both metrics rise as temperature increases, with shaded uncertainty bands. The visible finding is that higher temperature increases both 2-Wasserstein distance and MMD after an initial low-temperature minimum.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 5: Comparison of the ground truth data and model-generated data, colored by Leiden labels. For the generated data, the Leiden labels are predicted by an MLP classifier trained on the ground truth. Both variants of CaLMFlow successfully generate data spanning all clusters and closely align with the ground truth distribution. In contrast, while CFM, CFM-OT, and CFM-SB generate data across all classes, they fail to differentiate between them, indicating a mismatch in the underlying community structures. Models such as scVI, scGPT, and CPA are unable to generate data for some classes altogether.

Multi-panel scatter/embedding plot comparing methods on clustered single-cell-like data. The figure has nine panels labeled (a) Ground Truth, (b) CaLMFlow (R.I.), (c) CaLMFlow (N.L.), (d) CFM, (e) CFM-OT, (f) CFM-SB, (g) scVI, (h) scGPT, and (i) CPA. Each panel shows colored point clouds with a legend of class labels, generally numbered 0-7, though some panels show fewer labels.

No explicit axis titles or numeric ticks are visible. The visual quantity shown is a low-dimensional embedding or generated distribution of samples colored by cell/type cluster labels. The main visible finding is that different methods reproduce the ground-truth cluster structure with varying fidelity: CaLMFlow variants and some CFM variants retain mixed labeled structures, while scVI and scGPT collapse or separate only a subset of labels, and CPA produces elongated trajectory-like clusters rather than the compact ground-truth arrangement.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 6: Comparison of UMAPs of generated versus ground truth single-cell data between CFM and CaLMFlow. For each model, we generated 20,000 cells and plotted a UMAP with 20,000 randomly sampled cells from the immune cell dataset from Dong et al. (2023). The plots demonstrate that CaLMFlow produces a single-cell distribution more accurately reflecting the ground truth data, in contrast to CFM.

The figure appears to show low-dimensional projections of biomedical data, likely comparing synthetic/generated samples against original samples. In `(a) CFM`, generated and original points overlap partially but with visible separation around the main cluster. In `(b) CaLMFlow`, generated and original points appear more intermingled across multiple clusters, suggesting better distributional alignment.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 7: Comparison of conditional generation quality across different models for single-cell perturbation data. CaLMFlow (7b and (7c) generates data that accurately reflects the ground truth distribution across all combinatorial labels (cell type, perturbation, and chronicity), demonstrating its superior ability to understand complex conditions while maintaining a realistic overall data distribution. In contrast, methods like CFM-OT (7e), CFM-SB (7f), and scVI (7g) generate data where labels are blended, indicating an inability to comprehend conditions. While CFM (7d) and scGPT (7h) produce well-separated data, it's easily observed that this does not realistically represent the actual distribution when compared to the ground truth. For CaLMFlow, R.I. refers to randomly initialized CLM, and N.L. refers to natural language pretrained CLM.

routes.source_object_verbatim: 10,750 blood samples from public DNAm profiling GEO experiments
transformation_chain_verbatim: averaged P3GPT embeddings of the 50 most methylated genes for each sample
stacked the embeddings with a matrix of average ß-values on the promoters of 360 genes selected by SHAP importance
routes.insertion_or_fusion_verbatim: P3GPT embeddings used as features for downstream CatBoost predictor training
routes.evidence_quote: To illustrate the utility of P3GPT in aging research, we tested it as an age predictor trained on a collection of 10,750 blood samples from public DNAm profiling GEO experiments. To build the clock, we first averaged P3GPT embeddings of the 50 most methylated genes for each sample to obtain 360 dimensions-long vectors. Then we stacked the embeddings with a matrix of average ß-values on the promoters of 360 genes selected as the features with the highest SHAP importance scores in a CatBoost model trained on the ß-values of all 25,332 genes.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1.  P3GPT features a novel architecture enabling efficient omics-data training and multimodal extensions.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture schematic for a multimodal biomedical AI model. It shows model input combining instruction tokens, OMICs data, and annotation matrices; a modality mapper processing OMICs features; optional text data and knowledge graph data mapped into shared embeddings; then learnable embeddings and multimodal input passed into stacked transformer blocks.

Visible labels include OMICs modalities such as transcriptomics, epigenetics, and proteomics; components such as FF, B.Norm, ReLU, MHA, ALiBi, transformer blocks, and frozen weights. A novelty box claims integration of multimodal OMICs, knowledge graph, and text, plus a new tokenization method for OMICs data and language-model-style task solving. No quantitative experimental result or plot axes are shown.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture diagram for an AI-driven biomedical research system. It shows roles such as Data curator, Investigator, Lab technician, and Scholar interacting with datasets, a database, “Precious-3 GPT,” a robotics lab, and “Science42: DORA.” Green dashed arrows indicate data retrieval, hypothesis generation, lab validation requests, experimental data generation, academic text production, and pain-point discovery.

The database panel lists domains including species, omics, tissues, cell lines, compounds, diseases, and demographics; omics/modalities include DNAm, expression, proteomics, tabular omics, knowledge graph, and text. Source logos include TCGA, PubMed, LINCS, ARCHS4, GEO, PandaOmics, CCLE, GTEx, UK Biobank, and INDRA.

A research areas panel lists drug discovery, natural compound modeling, omics interpretation, and geroprotector discovery. The main visible message is an integrated loop where curated biomedical datasets train a GPT model, which proposes hypotheses, drives robotic experiments, and produces scientific text for further research iteration.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure with quantitative plots evaluating an age-prediction or gene-expression model, labeled panels A-F.

Panel A shows histograms of human age groups and mouse age groups, with counts in thousands on the y-axis and age bins on the x-axis. Sample sizes are shown: human N = 18,224 and mouse N = 23,024.

Panel B shows a bar plot of the top-20 tissue counts, with breast, prostate, lung, kidney, and liver among the most frequent tissues.

Panel C shows training and evaluation cross-entropy loss curves over steps, with both curves decreasing and stabilizing around 6.2.

Panel D shows boxplots of Jaccard similarity for upregulated and downregulated genes, comparing P3GPT, GPT4o, and random models. P3GPT appears higher than GPT4o and random, with significance markers.

Panel E compares predicted versus actual human age for Horvathv1 and P3GPT using density plots. P3GPT shows stronger alignment with the diagonal and higher reported correlation, R² = 0.90, than Horvathv1, R² = 0.54.

Panel F is a Pearson correlation heatmap among age-related predictors or clocks, including Horvathv1, Hannum, Lin, PhenoAge, DunedinPACE, DNAmGrimAge, and P3GPT-based. The P3GPT-based measure correlates most strongly with Horvathv1 among the displayed clocks.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 4. P3GPT shows unique capabilities, such as age prediction in unseen species, discovery of novel geroprotectors, and cross-omics target discovery.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure with experimental data and summary visualization.

Panel A: Scatter plot comparing `Actual age, years/lifespan` on the x-axis with `Predicted age, years/lifespan` on the y-axis. Points are colored by mammalian species and marked by tissue type, with a pink overall trendline. The visible finding is a positive relationship between actual normalized age and predicted normalized age across many tissues/species.

Panel B: Dose-response line plot labeled `XL-888`, showing `N total cells (relative to DMSO)` versus `Log10(M)`. Two conditions are plotted, `siNC` and `siβPIX`, with error bars. Cell number decreases with increasing XL-888 concentration, with the `siβPIX` condition appearing lower than control at tested doses.

Panel C: Venn diagram comparing categories `Proteome`, `Transcriptome`, and `Methylation`, plus a separate `None` circle. Overlaps are labeled with counts; the central overlap among all three is `7`, and `None` is `9`. The diagram summarizes overlap of detected/validated items across molecular data types.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 5. P3GPT uses a rigid prompt structure to formalize research settings and communicate with the user.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Two-panel workflow/model figure. Panel A shows a text-prompt style biomedical query with tagged fields such as `<drug> UNKNOWN`, species `m. musculus`, tissue `muscle`, datatype `expression`, up-regulated genes `ORM2 DEFB4B`, down-regulated genes `MUC5AC TBC1D3E MSMB`, and instruction `diff2cpd`; the output lists candidate drugs `metformin`, `semaglutide`, and `acarbose`.

Panel B diagrams a Precious3GPT workflow. The left box shows an input comparison between control age group `20-30 years` and case age group `70-80 years` using an `age2diff` instruction, producing up- and down-regulated gene lists. These gene lists are then passed into another Precious3GPT prompt with a `diff2compound` instruction to output a list of potential geroprotectors.

Main visible finding: the figure illustrates a model pipeline that converts age-associated gene expression differences into candidate anti-aging/geroprotective compounds.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture diagram for a multimodal biomedical transformer model. The figure shows model input composed of instruction tokens, OMICs features grouped as upregulated/downregulated/annotation matrices, plus OMICs data, text data, and knowledge graph data. A green “Modality Mapper (MM)” maps knowledge graph token embeddings from `[n × k]` to `[n × 256]`, with smaller MM modules for text and KG inputs.

The central panels show “Learnable embeddings” and “Multi-modal input” with stacked colored token blocks of dimension `×256`, including frozen and trainable indicators. The right side shows transformer blocks with ALiBi attention, MHA, normalization, feed-forward layers, and repeated block stacks labeled `×32`; one path is marked frozen weights and another trainable/frozen distinction with flame/snowflake icons.

A legend defines ALiBi, MHA, FF, and B.Norm. A “Novelty” list claims combined modalities: multimodal OMICs, knowledge graph, and text; a new OMICs tokenization method; language-model-style task solving; and a unique multiomics multispecies dataset. No quantitative plot axes or experimental results are shown; the main content is the proposed model architecture and multimodal input pipeline.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Bar plot/histogram panel labeled “A” showing the distribution of human age groups. The title reads “Human age groups” with “N = 18,224”. The x-axis is labeled “Age, years” with binned age ranges from 0-10 through 90-100, and the y-axis is labeled “Counts, k”. Light blue bars show counts per age bin. The highest counts are in middle-aged groups, roughly 40-65 years, with lower counts at the youngest and oldest age ranges.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Line plot panel labeled “C” showing cross-entropy loss versus training steps. The x-axis is “Steps, k” and the y-axis is “Cross-entropy loss.” A legend indicates two cohorts: Training in blue and Evaluation in orange. Both curves drop steeply at early steps and then gradually converge/plateau around ~6.2 loss by ~500k steps, with training and evaluation closely matched after the initial phase.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Box-and-strip plot panel labeled “D” showing Jaccard similarity for genes. The y-axis is “Jaccard similarity”; the x-axis groups genes into “Upregulated” and “Downregulated.” A legend compares three models: P3GPT in purple, GPT4o in salmon/red, and Random in green. Both gene groups show P3GPT with the highest Jaccard similarity, GPT4o intermediate, and Random lowest. Significance brackets with asterisks indicate statistically significant differences between model comparisons.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Two-panel density/contour scatter plot comparing predicted age versus actual age in years. Panel labels show “Horvathy1” and “P3GPT.” Both panels have x-axis “Actual age, years” and y-axis “Predicted age, years,” with dashed diagonal reference lines indicating perfect prediction. Color legends labeled “Counts” show point density.

The figure measures age prediction performance. Horvathy1 reports R² = 0.54, N = 2,206, while P3GPT reports R² = 0.90, N = 2,824. The visible finding is that P3GPT predictions align much more closely with actual age than Horvathy1, indicating substantially better age-prediction accuracy.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Heatmap/correlation matrix panel labeled “F” showing Pearson’s r values among biological age or epigenetic aging predictors: Horvathv1, Hannum, Lin, PhenoAge, DunedinPACE, DNAmGrimAge, and P3GPT-based. Both axes list the same predictors, with a blue-to-red legend for Pearson’s r from about 0.2 to 1.0. The diagonal is 1.00. Strong correlations are visible among Hannum, Lin, PhenoAge, and DNAmGrimAge, while DunedinPACE shows lower correlations with several clocks. P3GPT-based correlates strongly with Horvathv1 (0.81) but weakly to moderately with most others.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Figure type: workflow/model architecture schematic.

Visible panels/labels: Two Precious3GPT diagrams. Left panel shows “Age group (month) 20-60 years” and “Age group (year) 20-60 years” inputs feeding a “regulon-GPT transformer.” Right panel shows a model output pipeline with “Model output,” “UP-regulated genes: gene A, B, C,” “DOWN-regulated genes: X, Y, Z,” then predicted “UP-regulated genes: X, Y, Z” and “DOWN-regulated genes: A, B, C,” feeding an “scGPT/component transformer.”

Quantity shown: Gene regulation direction prediction, specifically up-regulated and down-regulated gene sets.

Main visible finding: The schematic illustrates Precious3GPT transforming age-related inputs and gene regulation lists into predicted opposite regulation gene sets through transformer-based modules.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: Overview of this work. Cell-o1 achieves state-of-the-art on the CellPuzzles task.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel schematic and results figure for the “CellPuzzles” task and “Cell-o1” training strategy. Left panel compares previous LLM-based cell type annotation, requiring no reasoning, with a CellPuzzles batch-level task requiring assignment of unique cell types using expressed genes and donor context, showing example reasoning for cell types such as CD4-positive alpha-beta T cell, CD8-positive alpha-beta T cell, capillary endothelial cell, plasma cell, and respiratory basal cell.

Middle panel shows the Cell-o1 training strategy with two stages: reasoning distillation, where candidate reasoning is accepted or rejected, and reinforcement learning using a policy model, reference model, reward function, KL term, group computation, and generated answers/rewards.

Right panel contains radial bar-style result plots for cell-level accuracy and batch-level accuracy. A legend compares models including Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama3.3-70B-Instruct, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, o3-mini, o1, and Cell-o1. The main visible finding is that Cell-o1 has the highest reported accuracy: 0.68 cell-level accuracy, marked +5.65%, and 0.33 batch-level accuracy, marked +73.05%.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 2: CellPuzzles formulates cell type annotation as a batch-level reasoning task that integrates gene expression and contextual metadata, inspired by how experts annotate cells in practice.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/comparison schematic with two horizontal panels. The top panel shows a conventional human expert task: input cell clusters with representative marker genes, an expert assigns cell type labels, and output labels include Pulmonary Alveolar Type 2 cells, CD8+ Cytotoxic T Cells, Lung Pericyte, Alveolar Macrophages, and Plasma Cells. The bottom panel shows a “CellPuzzles Task”: given a batch of N cells with contextual metadata and candidate cell types, a model reasons jointly from top expressed genes and cluster/cell relations to determine optimal label assignment, producing labels such as CD4-positive alpha-beta T Cell, CD8-positive alpha-beta T Cell, Smooth Muscle Cell, Lung Macrophage, Non-classical Monocyte, Capillary Endothelial Cell, Plasma Cell, and Respiratory Basal Cell. No axes or quantitative plots are present; the main point is illustrating cell type annotation as a reasoning/assignment workflow.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 3: Data distribution of CellPuzzles . (A) Age group distribution with male-female breakdown. (B) Sample distribution across a wide range of disease conditions. (C) Number of unique cell types observed across different tissues. For clarity, only the top 20 entries are shown in (B) and (C).
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel quantitative plot figure with three labeled panels:

(A) Horizontal age-group distribution with sex breakdown. X-axis is sample count; Y-axis is age group in years from 0-9 to 80-89. Beige horizontal bars show total age distribution, with small male/female pie markers or overlays; legend indicates Male in blue, Female in pink, Age in beige. Largest visible group is 60-69, followed by 70-79.

(B) Horizontal bar chart titled “Sample Distribution across Diseases.” X-axis is sample count; Y-axis lists disease categories including lung adenocarcinoma, chronic obstructive disease, normal, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary fibrosis, B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, sarcoidosis, pneumonia, and others. Lung adenocarcinoma has the highest sample count, with chronic obstructive disease and normal also high.

(C) Horizontal bar chart titled “Number of Unique Cell Types per Tissue.” X-axis is unique cell type count; Y-axis lists tissues including ileum, lung, blood, duodenum, colon, bone marrow, nose, sigmoid colon, descending colon, transverse colon, lymph node, brain, jejunum, kidney, liver, pleural effusion, and adrenal tissue. Ileum has the most unique cell types, followed by lung and blood/duodenum.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 4: Fine-grained analysis of model performance. (A) Cell-level and batch-level accuracy across varying numbers of cells per batch. (B) Distribution of per-batch cell-level accuracy across models.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel performance comparison figure with plots. Panel (A) contains two radar/spider charts: “Cell-level Acc by Number of Cells per Batch” and “Batch-level Acc by Number of Cells per Batch,” with spokes labeled 8–15 cells per batch and model legend including Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama3.3-70B-Instruct, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, o3-mini, o1, and Cell-o1. Panel (B) is a violin/box distribution plot titled “Per-batch Cell-level Acc Distribution,” with y-axis “Per-batch Cell-level Accuracy” and x-axis model names.

The measured quantity is cell-level and batch-level accuracy across different language/model systems. The main visible finding is that Cell-o1 and o1 show the highest accuracy distributions and radar values, while smaller/open models such as Llama3.1-8B-Instruct perform much lower.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 5: Comparing training and inference dynamics across different configurations.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel experimental results plot with four conditions labeled (A)–(D). Each condition shows two stacked line charts over training steps/iterations from 0 to 1000. Legends describe reinforcement-learning fine-tuning setups using base model “w/ SFT,” RL method GRPO or PPO, and reward type “Batch Reward” or “Cell & Batch Reward.”

Visible axes include red left y-axes for “Training Reward” or “Test Performance,” and blue right y-axes for “Response Length.” Top panels plot training reward with shaded variability and response length; bottom panels plot test performance and response length at evaluation points.

Main visible finding: condition (D), using GRPO with “Cell & Batch Reward,” shows the strongest and most stable increase in training reward and relatively higher test performance. Condition (B) remains near-zero in reward/performance while response length increases sharply late in training. Condition (C) with PPO shows noisy reward and declining response length.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 6: Analysis of model reasoning behavior. (A) Step-by-step reasoning traces generated by each model for the same task. (B) Expert evaluation of reasoning quality comparing Cell-o1 with baseline models. (C) Proportion of traces exhibiting self-reflection and curriculum reasoning behaviors.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing a comparison of cell-type annotation/reasoning by different LLMs. Panels include:

(A) Workflow-style/table-like examples comparing predicted cell assignments for `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct`, `GPT-4o`, `o1`, and `Cell-o1`, with labels such as “Right Prediction,” “Wrong Prediction,” “Incorrect Reasoning,” “No Reasoning,” and “Plausible but Incorrect.” It shows cell-by-cell analysis and final assignments for intestinal/goblet/plasma/T-cell examples.

(B) Horizontal stacked bar chart comparing outcomes across models, with categories “Model wins,” “Tie,” and “Cell-o1 wins.” Cell-o1 visibly wins most comparisons against GPT-4o and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, while results against o1 are more balanced.

(C) Two bar charts labeled “Self-Reflection Reasoning” and “Curriculum Reasoning,” showing proportions (%) for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, GPT-4o, o1, and Cell-o1. Cell-o1 has the highest visible proportions, especially for curriculum reasoning, while other models are near zero or lower.

Main visible finding: the proposed `Cell-o1` approach appears to outperform or provide richer reasoning than baseline LLMs for cell-type assignment in the displayed examples and summary comparisons.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/schema panel for single-cell gene expression annotation. It shows a batch of donor-derived cells with donor metadata, a gene expression matrix/heatmap labeled “Gene Expression Profiles,” contextual metadata text, and a “Top Expressed Genes” list per cell.

Visible labels include tissue, disease, age, sex, smoking status, cell IDs, gene columns, and top gene examples such as S100A9, TMSB10, RPL37, RPL18A, MALAT1, FTL, B2M, CD74, and immunoglobulin genes. The biological quantities shown are cell-level gene expression profiles and associated donor/sample metadata. The main visible message is that combining gene expression with context metadata supports cell-specific interpretation, illustrated by a male 68-year-old lung adenocarcinoma donor.
