figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the Cell2Text framework. The model takes single-cell RNA-seq profiles as input and processes them through a pretrained Geneformer encoder to generate contextualized gene-level embeddings. These embeddings are projected into the semantic space of the language model via a lightweight adapter module, aligning biological signals with linguistic representations. A pretrained, instruction-tuned LLM decoder then generates structured natural language descriptions that capture cellular identity, tissue of origin, disease associations, and pathway activity.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Model architecture/workflow diagram for generating or modeling single-cell descriptions from gene expression and metadata. It shows a cell with genes `Gene Z`, `Gene E`, ..., `Gene C` passed through a “cell encoder” to produce gene embeddings, then a “modality adapter” projecting dimensions labeled `+512`, `2048`, `3072`. These embeddings are combined with instruction embeddings and prompt embeddings as input to a language model decoder.

Left side lists cell metadata such as cell type, developmental stage, disease, sex, tissue, and pathway annotations, which form a textual cell description `Cp`. Bottom right shows next-token probability `p`, with the training objective labeled `Lsft = LCrossEntropy(Cp, p)`. Main visible point: the figure illustrates a supervised fine-tuning pipeline aligning single-cell gene/modal embeddings with text generation through a language model decoder.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 2: Token length distribution of gene expression sequences after tokenization with the Geneformer tokenizer.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Histogram plot titled “Length Distribution - combined” showing frequency versus sequence/text length. The x-axis is labeled “Length” and spans roughly 0 to 4100; the y-axis is labeled “Frequency” and reaches about 100,000. A legend marks a red dashed vertical line as “Mean: 1843.2”. The distribution is broad, with many observations between about 300 and 2500, tapering toward longer lengths, plus a very large spike near length ~4000, suggesting many entries are capped or clustered at the maximum length.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 3: Token length distribution of natural language descriptions after tokenization with the Llama-3.21B-Instruct tokenizer.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Histogram plot showing the distribution of tokenized `natural_desc` lengths for a combined dataset. The x-axis is labeled `# tokens`, and the y-axis is `Frequency`. Light green bars show counts across token-length bins, with a red dashed vertical line marking the mean. The legend reports `Mean: 104.3`. Most descriptions cluster around roughly 70-120 tokens, with a right-skewed tail extending past 200 tokens and sparse values approaching 300.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 4: Overview of the distribution of cell types in the dataset. For clarity, only the 30 most abundant categories out of 783 are shown.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Bar chart showing category counts for biomedical cell types. The y-axis is labeled “Count” and ranges to about 30,000; the x-axis is labeled “Categories” with rotated cell-type labels. Bars are ordered descending and colored with a blue-to-red gradient.

The highest-count categories are oligodendrocyte (~29,725), neuron (~27,981), CA4-positive alpha-beta T cell (~21,994), fibroblast (~20,957), granulocyte/monocyte (~20,220), CD8-positive alpha-beta T cell (~19,635), and T cell (~18,755). Lower visible categories include plasma cell, mural cell, and stromal cell (~5,647). The main finding is a strongly imbalanced distribution of annotated cell categories, dominated by oligodendrocytes and neurons.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 5: Overview of the distribution of disease categories in the dataset. For clarity, only the 30 most abundant categories out of 128 are shown.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Bar chart showing the top 30 categories for `final_combined_disease_top_values` on a log-scaled y-axis. The x-axis is labeled “Categories” and lists disease/condition categories; the y-axis is labeled “Count (Log Scale).” Bars are annotated with counts.

Main visible finding: the category `normal` dominates with 592,932 counts, followed by `COVID-19` with 61,961. Other high-frequency categories include `pulmonary disease`, `tuberculosis`, `lung adenocarcinoma`, `squamous lung cell carcinoma`, `malignant ovarian germ cell tumor`, `dementia`, `coronary disease`, and `breast cancer`, each far lower than the top two.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 6: Overview of the distribution of tissue (general) categories in the dataset. For clarity, only the 30 most abundant categories out of 347 are shown.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Bar chart showing the top 30 categories in `final_combined_tissue_general_top_values` on a logarithmic y-axis. The x-axis is labeled `Categories`, and the y-axis is `Count (Log Scale)`. Each bar has a numeric count label.

The plotted categories appear to be tissue/general anatomical terms, including brain, blood, lung, eye, breast, heart, kidney, liver, small intestine, skin of body, colon, bone marrow, placenta, endocrine gland, respiratory system, musculature, nose, pancreas, adipose tissue, reproductive system, intestine, stomach, digestive system, endocrine gland, lymph node, vasculature, prostate gland, uterus, mucosa, and adrenal gland.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel workflow/model architecture figure for a biomedical AI paper. Panels are labeled **a–d**.

- **Panel a:** Compares two strategies: training a foundation model from scratch from single-omics data using tokenization, LLM architecture, and pretraining, versus fine-tuning existing NLP LLMs for CellHermes using multiple omics data, textualization, and fine-tuning.
- **Panel b:** Shows emulation of self-supervised learning with question-answer prompts. No quantitative axes or plotted experimental measurements are visible; the main content is a conceptual workflow describing CellHermes training tasks and downstream uses.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: CellTosg2Sequence overall workflow. Raw scRNA-seq expression profiles are ranked into a Cell Sentence (topK =200 HGNC gene symbols in descending expression order). A heterogeneous biomedical KG assembled from 11 public databases is encoded by a 2-layer R-GCN with RotatE scoring and projected into 5120-dim virtual tokens via the KGProjector MLP. The virtual tokens are prepended to the textual prompt (cell sentence + metadata + task instruction) and fed into the Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct backbone. The same checkpoint handles cell-type annotation (CTA), perturbation prediction (CPA), and gene-perturbation significance (PSA) through a unified text-in / text-out interface.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture schematic for “CellTosg2Sequence Overall WorkFlow.” The figure shows a pipeline from raw RNA-seq data and biological prior knowledge databases through an LLM agent quality-control/filter step, graph training using R-GCN encoder plus RotatE decoder/scorer, construction of a rich knowledge graph with neighborhood attention, and injection of a virtual embedding into an LLM prompt.

Visible labels include “Raw RNAseq Data,” “Biological Prior Knowledge in 11 entities from Public Databases,” “Cell Sentence Arrangement in Prompt,” “Example of Original Embedding Style,” “Final Prompt,” and “Virtual Embedding Injection.” The RNA-seq portion shows a small expression-profile heatmap for Cell 1, Cell 2, Cell 3, and Cell N. The knowledge sources listed include Protein, UniProt, HGNC, STRING v12, Pathway, Reactome, TRRUST, Drug, DrugBank, ChEMBL, Gene, HGNC, Disease, DisGeNET/Open Targets, TF, DoRothEA, and TRRUST.

The main visible idea is that cell/gene ranking information and biological knowledge graph embeddings are combined to enrich LLM prompts for cell-type and perturbation-related question answering, with examples involving K562 cells, Gene A/B/C, and B-cell marker IGHM.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 3: Graph injection pipeline (schematic). Step 1 : Raw scRNA-seq expression is read per gene. Step 2 : Genes are ranked by expression into a cell sentence. Step 3 : The topK genes (plus perturbation conditions such as drug, time, and dose) are used to select their corresponding subgraph node vectors from the frozen KG entity table. Step 4 : Node vectors are passed through the KGProjector MLP (256 → 5120 → 5120, SiLU; see ğ3.3) to produce virtual tokens matching the LM embedding dimension. Step 5 : Virtual tokens are prepended to the textual token sequence in the LM embedding space. Step 6 : The model performs inference under task-specific metrics and ontology-hierarchy reward.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture schematic for a biomedical machine-learning method. It has six labeled panels:

1. RNA-seq reading by gene, showing a single-cell input plus perturbation context: Gefitinib, 4 h, 5.0 µM, with gene expression bars labeled g1–g10.
2. “Cell Sentence of topK Gene descending order,” listing genes such as MT-CO1, MT-ND4, RPS27, B2M, ACTB, GAPDH.
3. Subgraph gene selection with node vectors, showing a graph/network with selected drug and top-K gene nodes; legend marks drug selected in green and genes top-K selected in red. Side boxes show gene tokens, drug/time/dose tokens, and drug description.
4. Transformation of node vectors into projector MLP virtual tokens matching LLM dimension, with dimensions labeled 256, 1024, GELU, 2048, GELU, and output 4096 virtual tokens.
5. Integration into LLM vector embedding space, combining virtual tokens with text tokens such as “What cell is this?”
6. Inference and validation under metrics and reward models, illustrated by a bar chart and rising arrow.

Main visible content: a pipeline converting single-cell RNA-seq and drug perturbation metadata into graph-selected gene/drug representations, projecting them into LLM-compatible embeddings for downstream inference and validation.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 4: Stage-II KG-anchor training. The KG entity table E feeds virtual tokens through the KGProjector into the LM backbone; the mean last-layer hidden state at KG-injection positions forms z KG i . A learned projection matrix W aligns z KG i toward the frozen label-string embeddings e label i via L anchor (Eq. 3, τ =0 . 07 ). The gene-anchor loss L gene (Eq. 4) simultaneously aligns position-level hidden states z i,k with frozen gene embeddings e gene g i,k .

The diagram compares mean-pooled last-layer hidden vectors for KG injection positions and label string positions, applies a matrix H to transform one representation, and uses backpropagation in stages I and II to update parameters. Checkmark icons indicate matched/desired representations. The main visible finding is methodological: aligning KG node embeddings with text label embeddings for biomedical entity representation learning.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel data summary figure showing dataset composition for a single-cell biomedical study.

Panel A is a pie chart labeled “Train / Val / Test Split (total = 3.37M cells)” with train, validation, and test partitions. The train split dominates at about 3.02M cells, 89.4%, while validation and test are each about 178K cells, 5.3%.

Panel B is a pie chart labeled “Sequencing Technology Distribution (training split, 9 platforms)” with a legend for sequencing platforms. The largest category is 10x Chromium 3' v3 at 50%, followed by 10x Chromium 3' v2 at 23%, then smaller platform fractions including 10x Chromium 5', Smart-seq2, sci-RNA-seq3, MARS-seq, SPLiT-seq, BD Rhapsody, and Other.

Panel C is a histogram labeled “Cell-Type Class Imbalance (865 types)” with x-axis “Cell count per type [log10]” and y-axis “Number of cell types.” A red dashed vertical line marks a training cap of 15,000 cells. The visible finding is strong class imbalance: many cell types have fewer than 5,000 cells, while a small number are very abundant, including a labeled maximum around 500,000 cells.

Panel D is a horizontal bar chart labeled “Top-10 Tissue Contributions (training split; 70 tissues total)” with x-axis “Cells (x1,000).” Brain and blood contribute the most cells, followed by eye, lung, breast, heart, kidney, liver, intestine, and colon.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1 . Overview of the CellWhisperer multimodal AI for natural-language analysis of transcriptome data
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel workflow and result figure for a biomedical AI model, CellWhisperer, linking transcriptome embeddings with natural-language text.

Panel a shows a model/training schematic: datasets from GEO metadata, ARCHS4 bulk RNA-seq, and single-cell annotations are converted into sample descriptions and conversations using LLMs; transcriptome and language encoders are trained into a shared 2048-dimensional multimodal embedding space. The application area shows free-text cell labeling and chat-based querying of cell samples.

Panel b shows a UMAP landscape labeled “An annotated landscape of human transcriptomes,” with many colored clusters representing 705,430 GEO transcriptomes in CellWhisperer embedding space.

Panel c shows a UMAP query result for the term “leukemia,” colored by a CellWhisperer score legend from negative blue to positive red. Red-enriched regions indicate transcriptomes matching the leukemia query.

Panel d shows three small histograms of GEO submission dates for selected queried sample groups, including activated myeloid differentiation in HSPCs, K562 erythroleukemia cells in culture, and obese adipose tissue immune/metabolic state.

Main visible finding: the model organizes large-scale human transcriptome data into a shared language-transcriptome embedding space that supports natural-language search, labeling, and biological sample exploration.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 2 . Evaluation of the CellWhisperer model by zero-shot prediction of cell types, diseases, and tissues 600
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing zero-shot cell type prediction performance for CellWhisperer on scRNA-seq datasets.

Figure type: workflow schematic plus UMAP visualizations, confusion-matrix-like heatmap, and bar plots.

Panels:
- **a**: Workflow for evaluating zero-shot cell type prediction. A labeled scRNA-seq evaluation dataset is shown as a UMAP, with a free-text query such as “erythrocytes”; prediction is evaluated against expert-annotated ground-truth cell types using CellWhisperer scores.
- **b**: Zero-shot prediction performance on Tabula Sapiens. Left shows UMAPs comparing Tabula Sapiens annotation versus CellWhisperer prediction. Right shows a heatmap/confusion matrix for 20 common cell types, with labels such as erythrocyte, macrophage, monocyte, neutrophil, NK cell, T cell subtypes, B cell, epithelial cell, goblet cell, basal cell, and hepatocyte.
- **c**: Bar chart summary of zero-shot performance across prediction tasks, reporting ROC-AUC and accuracy for Tabula Sapiens, pancreas, ImmGen, and disease validation datasets, with random baseline indicated.
- **d**: Bar plots of ROC-AUC and accuracy for selected cell attributes, including cell type, organ/tissue, and disease subtype.

Main visible finding: CellWhisperer shows above-random zero-shot prediction performance across multiple cell type and attribute prediction tasks, with strong ROC-AUC values but variable accuracy depending on dataset and label type.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 3 . Interactive chat-based exploration of scRNA-seq data using CellWhisperer 615
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing an interactive single-cell transcriptomics exploration workflow for the Tabula Sapiens dataset using CellWhisperer.

Figure type: workflow/interface screenshot plus UMAP/scatter plots and chat-based annotation panels.

Panels:
- **a**: Screenshot-style interface labeled “CellWhisperer exploration of the Tabula Sapiens dataset,” showing a UMAP-like embedding, a CellWhisperer score histogram, score-based and visual cell selection, and a chat box.
- **b**: Large UMAP/scatter plot titled “Cell annotation with free-text query ‘structural cells with immune functions’.” Points are colored by CellWhisperer score with a blue-to-red legend ranging roughly from -8 to 8. Several regions are annotated with inferred cell/tissue descriptions such as macrophages, endothelium, stromal cells, epithelial cells, pericytes, and fibroblasts from decidua tissue.
- **c**: Chat protocol panel where the user asks about selected cells and immune functions; CellWhisperer responses describe fibroblasts from decidua tissue and mention genes/pathways including COL1A1, COL3A1, COL1A2, MMP1, MMP2, HSPA1A/HSPB1/HSP90AA1, IFITM3, ISG15, JUN, FOS, CCL2, CXCL8, IL6, and extracellular matrix remodeling.
- **d**: UMAP/scatter plot titled “Mean expression of the genes mentioned by CellWhisperer,” with a green-to-blue/purple expression legend labeled expression log, highlighting the selected cell cluster.

Measured/shown quantity: CellWhisperer text-query scores and mean expression of genes mentioned in the chat response across single-cell UMAP embeddings.

Main visible finding: a free-text query for “structural cells with immune functions” selects a specific fibroblast-like decidua-associated cell region, and genes discussed by CellWhisperer show elevated mean expression in the selected cell cluster.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 4 . Interactive exploration of user-provided scRNA-seq data with CellWhisperer
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing a workflow and example results for **CellWhisperer** analysis of a user-provided scRNA-seq dataset.

Panels:
- **a**: Workflow diagram for processing user-provided scRNA-seq data into a CellWhisperer-ready H5AD dataset with embeddings and cluster labels, followed by local or web/cloud interactive exploration.
- **b**: UMAP embedding of single cells labeled with inferred biological cell-state descriptions, including intestinal epithelial, goblet, tuft, immune, erythrocyte, and proliferating transit-amplifying cell populations.
- **c**: UMAP-like scatter plot for the query **“Show me stem cells”**, colored by **CellWhisperer score** with a blue-to-red scale.
- **d**: Chat protocol text box describing the top-scoring cells for the stem-cell query, mentioning an **LGR5-expressing stem cell subpopulation**.
- **e**: Gene-expression UMAP for **LGR5**, with a green-to-blue expression legend, supporting the queried stem-cell signal.
- **f**: Violin/box plot comparing **CellWhisperer scores** for the query “Show me stem cells” across **inflamed** versus **non-inflamed** dataset annotations, with a reported significance of **p < 1e-37**.

Main visible finding: CellWhisperer maps natural-language queries such as “stem cells” onto specific scRNA-seq cell populations, highlights high-scoring cells in UMAP space, links them to marker expression such as **LGR5**, and compares query scores across inflammation context.

figure_candidates.caption: Extended Data Figure 1 . CellWhisperer cross-modality retrieval performance and model ablation testing
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel experimental results figure with plots comparing model performance. Panel **a** shows cross-modality retrieval performance of a final model and during training on a disease validation dataset. The left bar chart reports **Recall at top n** for target modalities **text** and **transcriptomes**, with bars for recall at top **1, 5, 10, 50** matches; values increase with larger top-k, reaching about **0.97-0.98** at top 50. The adjacent line plot shows **Recall at top 5** versus **epoch**, fluctuating around roughly **0.53-0.62** after early improvement.

Panel **b** is a horizontal ablation/performance comparison titled **CellWhisperer ablation performance across five metrics**. Rows list model/training variants such as frozen LiT models, loss functions, batch size, transcriptome model, data sources, augmentation, sample weights, and **CellWhisperer**. The x-axis is **Normalized scores (fixed range 0-1)**. Colored points represent five metrics in the legend: Tabula sapiens zero-shot cell type classification, batch integration, cell type integration, disease validation retrieval, and per-single-cell classification. The visible finding is that performance varies across ablations, with **CellWhisperer** shown as the reference/final method across multiple metrics.

figure_candidates.caption: Extended Data Figure 2 . CellWhisperer batch integration performance and evaluation based on gene sets
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing evaluation of CellWhisperer against curated gene sets and single-cell integration benchmarks.

Panels:
- **a**: Workflow and validation schematic comparing CellWhisperer text-term scoring with GSVA gene set variation analysis. Includes scatter plot of CellWhisperer score vs GSVA score per gene set with Pearson correlation **0.52**, and cumulative distributions with signed KS statistic **0.5**.
- **b**: Violin/box-style distributions of signed KS-statistics across gene set libraries, labeled PanglaoDB, Augmented_2021, Tabula_Sapiens, Azimuth_2023, Disease OMIM Expanded, GO Biological Process 2023, and GO Molecular Function 2023. Shows mostly positive correspondence between CellWhisperer and GSVA scores.
- **c**: Disease-library correlation plot showing cumulative proportion vs correlation coefficient rho, with annotated disease terms such as “colorectal cancer,” “thyroid carcinoma,” “nephropathy,” “stature,” and “dyslexia.” Most correlations appear positive.
- **d**: Dataset integration performance evaluation with schematic examples and bar charts for **batch integration score** and **cell type clustering score**. CellWhisperer scores are higher than Geneformer in both shown metrics: batch integration **0.84 vs 0.78**, cell type clustering **0.56 vs 0.49**.

Main visible finding: CellWhisperer shows positive correspondence with curated gene-set activity scores and slightly better integration/clustering benchmark performance than Geneformer in the displayed comparisons.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow and result panel for evaluating a language model on transcriptome embeddings. Left: question-answer pairs from a test set (`n=200`) combine a “transcriptome embedding” with a prompt question (“Describe this sample”) and ground-truth answer (“These are bronchial epithelial…”), passed into an LLM layer. The model outputs a prediction scored by perplexity.

Middle: scatter/strip plot of perplexity values, with x-axis “Perplexity lower is better” ranging roughly from 1.51 to 14.25 and y-axis categories 1–5. Legend distinguishes gray “Mismatched embeddings (n=30)” and purple “Matched embedding.” 

Right: horizontal quantile plot labeled “Perplexity quantiles for all 200 test cases,” showing inverted perplexity quantiles from 0 to 1.0. The visible result emphasizes that matched embeddings tend to have better/lower perplexity quantiles than mismatched embeddings.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Horizontal bar plot showing model performance by cell-type label. The x-axis is labeled “Perplexity quantiles (inverted)” from 0.0 to 1.0, with a dashed vertical reference line around 0.5. The y-axis is labeled “Labels (Tabula sapiens (20 common cell types))” and lists natural-language cell identity prompts such as macrophage, memory B cell, type II pneumocyte, CD8-positive alpha-beta T cell, hepatocyte, monocyte, endothelial cell, NK cell, erythrocyte, and basophil.

Each label has a light green horizontal bar with dark error bars. Most cell types score above the 0.5 reference line, while some such as T cell, club cell, NK cell, and basophil are near or below it. The strongest visible values are for several T-cell and monocyte/endothelial-related labels near the upper end of the scale.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure describing a transcriptome-language embedding model/workflow called CellWhisperer. Panel a is a schematic workflow/model architecture: datasets of human transcriptomes and text are used to generate sample descriptions and training conversations, then a multimodal embedding space is trained with language model, transcriptome model, and LLM components, and applied to free-text cell labeling and chat-style querying of transcriptome data. It shows labeled sections for Dataset, Training, Inference, and Application, plus arrows between transcriptome/text inputs and outputs.

Panel b is a UMAP scatter plot labeled “Landscape of annotated human transcriptomes,” showing CellWhisperer embeddings of 705,430 transcriptomes from GEO, with many colored clusters. Axes are indicated as UMAP without numeric ticks.

Panel c is another UMAP-style query map labeled “Querying the human transcriptome landscape with natural language,” colored by CellWhisperer score for a text search term, with a blue-to-red color bar approximately from -10 to 10. Red and blue regions indicate transcriptomes matching or opposing the queried natural-language concepts.

Panel d shows small histogram/time-series panels of GEO submission dates for selected samples, with y-axis “Num. samples” and x-axis “GEO submission date” spanning roughly 2013 to 2023. Main visible finding: the model embeds large transcriptome collections into a searchable natural-language space, where text queries highlight biologically coherent transcriptome regions.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/result schematic for evaluating cell-type query scoring on an expert-annotated scRNA-seq dataset. Left panel shows a UMAP embedding of many colored cell clusters labeled “Expert-annotated scRNA-seq evaluation dataset (not used during training),” with an arrow pointing to a red-highlighted cluster labeled “Erythrocytes.” A “Free-text query for cell types” arrow leads to the right evaluation panel.

Right panel is labeled “Evaluation against expert-annotated cell types” and shows a query for “erythrocytes.” It contains a UMAP colored by “CellWhisperer score,” with red high-scoring cells corresponding to erythrocytes, and a density/histogram plot below with x-axis “CellWhisperer score,” y-axis “Density,” gray bars for “Other cell types,” and red bars for “Erythrocytes.” Main visible finding: erythrocytes receive distinctly higher CellWhisperer scores than other cell types for the erythrocyte text query.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel experiment result figure showing zero-shot prediction performance for common cell types. Left side has two UMAP scatter plots labeled “Tabula Sapiens annotation” and “CellWhisperer prediction,” with points colored by cell type. Right side is a heatmap/confusion-matrix-like plot titled “Tabula Sapiens (20 common cell types),” comparing expert-annotated cell classes against predicted cells, with a blue intensity legend labeled “Predicted cells per expert-annotated class (%)” from 0 to 80.

Cell types listed include erythrocyte, macrophage, monocyte, classical/non-classical monocyte, neutrophil, basophil, NK cell, CD8-positive alpha-beta T cell, CD4-positive alpha-beta memory T cell, B cell classes, capillary endothelial cell, type II pneumocyte, respiratory goblet cell, club cell, basal cell, and hepatocyte. The main visible finding is strong diagonal signal in the heatmap for many classes, indicating that CellWhisperer predictions largely match Tabula Sapiens annotations, with some off-diagonal confusion among related immune and epithelial/endothelial cell types.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure comparing a natural-language CellWhisperer single-cell RNA-seq analysis workflow with a conventional bioinformatics workflow. Panels include workflow diagrams, UMAP embeddings, query score maps, gene expression plots, chat output, differential expression ranking, and violin/box-like distributions.

Visible panels:
- **a**: CellWhisperer workflow from scRNA-seq h5ad input through automated processing to interactive exploration with AI cluster labels, cell search, and chat.
- **b**: UMAP with CellWhisperer-generated cluster labels for intestinal epithelial and immune-related cell populations.
- **c**: UMAP colored by CellWhisperer score for query “Show me stem cells.”
- **d**: Chat-style response describing a top-scoring “stem cells” subpopulation.
- **e**: UMAP showing expression of marker gene **LGR5**.
- **f**: Distribution of “stem cells” CellWhisperer score by inflammation status.
- **g**: Conventional bioinformatics workflow: integration, annotation, differential analysis, plotting.
- **h**: Raw vs integrated dataset UMAP, with legend for Healthy, Inflamed, Noninflamed.
- **i**: Cluster-level cell type annotation UMAP with labels including B cells, T cells, TA cells, colonocytes, BEST4+ epithelial, BEST2+ goblet cell.
- **j**: Cell-level annotation zoom highlighting stem cells.
- **k**: Differential expression rank plot for “Stem cells,” highlighting **LGR5** as significant.
- **l**: Stemness score distribution across cells by inflammation status, showing a significant difference.

Main visible finding: CellWhisperer appears to identify and describe stem-cell-like intestinal cell populations directly from scRNA-seq embeddings, with correspondence to known marker **LGR5** and comparison to conventional annotation/differential-expression workflows.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture diagram for a biomedical AI model. It shows paired transcriptome datasets feeding Geneformer and BioBERT encoders, producing normalized 2048-dimensional embeddings. A central matrix illustrates dot-product similarity with batch size 512 and an InfoNCE loss, including maximize/minimize regions. On the right, transcriptome-conversation paired datasets feed a Mistral 7B LLM with concatenated token embeddings for multimodal instruction tuning using cross-entropy loss on answer tokens. Labels include GEO and CELLxGENE Census data counts, Geneformer/BioBERT layer and parameter notes, frozen/unfrozen training stages, and conversation-type counts. The main visible finding is an architecture for aligning transcriptomic embeddings with language-model instruction tuning, not an experimental result plot.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Two-panel quantitative result figure from a human diseases dataset. Left panel is a grouped bar chart titled “Human Diseases dataset” showing “Recall at <top>” on the y-axis for two retrieved modalities on the x-axis: “Target” and “Transcriptomes.” Bars are grouped by recall-at-top matches 1, 5, 10, and 50, with legend in grayscale. Visible values increase with larger top-k: Target approximately 0.19, 0.55, 0.79, 0.97; Transcriptomes approximately 0.24, 0.59, 0.79, 0.98.

Right panel is a line plot titled “Human Diseases dataset” with x-axis “Epoch” and y-axis “Recall at top-5.” The curve rises from about 0.44 to around 0.58–0.62 early, then fluctuates around 0.53–0.57 across later epochs. Main finding: retrieval recall improves with larger top-k, and top-5 recall varies but remains around the mid-0.5 range after early training.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

A horizontal dot/strip plot comparing normalized scores across experimental settings for a CellWhisperer-related model. The x-axis is labeled “Normalized scores (fixed range 0-1)” from 0 to 1. The y-axis lists ablation/configuration factors including “LiT: Both models frozen,” “Loss function: JSD,” “LiT: Only language model frozen,” “LiT: Both models unfrozen,” “Batch size: 32, Grad. accum.: 16,” “Transcriptome model: scGPT,” “Data: Only GEO,” “Loss function: Mean(JSD, InfoNCE),” “Gradient accumulation: 16,” “Data: CELLxGENE Census,” “Augmentation: 2 annotation sets,” “Sample weights: Constant (1),” and “CellWhisperer embedding model.”

Colored dots show score distributions per condition, with gray horizontal bars indicating ranges or summaries. The bottom “CellWhisperer embedding model” row is highlighted in orange. Visibly, the embedding model and several ablation settings achieve mid-to-high normalized scores, while points vary broadly across metrics/configurations, with many values clustered around roughly 0.4-0.8 and some reaching near 1.0.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Bar-chart results figure with three stacked metric panels: Accuracy, F1 Score, and AUROC. The x-axis lists datasets/tasks: Tabula Sapiens, Tabula Sapiens (20 common cell types), Pancreas, ImmGen, and Asian Immune Diversity Atlas. Bars compare models from the legend: scGPT unfrozen with pseudo-bulks, scGPT frozen with pseudo-bulks and single cells, scGPT frozen with pseudo-bulks, CellWhisperer scGPT-based, and CellAssign. A side annotation groups scGPT/CellWhisperer as fine-tuned and CellAssign as zero-shot.

The figure reports cell-type or biological classification performance across datasets. Main visible finding: performance is low on Tabula Sapiens for Accuracy and F1 but high AUROC; for most other datasets AUROC is high across models, while CellWhisperer often has among the highest Accuracy/F1, especially on ImmGen and Asian Immune Diversity Atlas.

Grouped bar chart comparing model performance across datasets. It has three stacked metric panels labeled Accuracy, F1 Score, and AUROC, each with y-axis from 0.0 to 1.0. The x-axis lists datasets: Tabula Sapiens, Tabula Sapiens (20 common cell types), Pancreas, ImmGen, and Asian Immune Diversity Atlas.

Multi-panel workflow and results figure. Left panel shows an LLM expanding four “Annotation queries” about embryonic development stages into “Query variants,” indicated by colored dot groups and arrows, then feeding them into a “CellWhisperer embedding model.” Middle panel is a densMAP/UMAP scatter plot titled “densMAP of variant text embeddings,” with axes `UMAP 1` and `UMAP 2`; colored clusters correspond to query variants. SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel biomedical data figure showing validation of CellWhisperer-identified organ marker genes.

Figure type: composite of scatter plots, violin plots, gene set enrichment bubble plot, and spatial expression maps.

Panels:
- **a**: Scatter plots for organs including cerebrum, heart, intestine, kidney, liver, lung, muscle, pancreas, spleen, and stomach. X-axis shows marker gene z-score, y-axis shows CellWhisperer z-score across cells per day of development. Each panel reports correlation `r` and `p` value, with positive regression trends.
- **b**: Violin plots showing numbers of papers co-mentioning organ names with gene sets. Groups include CellWhisperer-identified marker genes, fetal gene expression atlas markers, shared marker genes, and random control genes. Odds ratios and p-values are annotated.
- **c**: Violin plots of paper co-mentions for organ-gene pairs grouped by expression enrichment bins, with “new” pairs highlighted in red for the high-enrichment group.
- **d**: Gene set enrichment for CellWhisperer-identified heart marker genes. Bubble plot lists muscle/cardiac-related GO terms and dilated cardiomyopathy; x-axis is combined score, color encodes adjusted p-value, and bubble size encodes fraction of genes in the set.
- **e**: Spatial expression maps of liver marker genes in a CS8 embryo, comparing established liver markers such as `HNF4A` and `FGA` with CellWhisperer-identified markers such as `REEP6` and `GOLT1A`.

Main visible finding: CellWhisperer organ scores correlate positively with established marker gene expression across organs, and its identified marker genes are enriched for organ-specific literature co-mentions and biologically relevant pathways, with spatial expression consistent with liver localization.

Workflow and results panel for evaluating transcriptome embeddings with a model labeled `CellWhisperer`. SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure describing a transcriptome-language embedding model/workflow called CellWhisperer. Panel a is a schematic workflow/model architecture: datasets of human transcriptomes and text are used to generate sample descriptions and training conversations, then a multimodal embedding space is trained with language model, transcriptome model, and LLM components, and applied to free-text cell labeling and chat-style querying of transcriptome data. It shows labeled sections for Dataset, Training, Inference, and Application, plus arrows between transcriptome/text inputs and outputs.

Panel b is a UMAP scatter plot labeled “Landscape of annotated human transcriptomes,” showing CellWhisperer embeddings of 705,430 transcriptomes from GEO, with many colored clusters. Axes are indicated as UMAP without numeric ticks.

Panel c is another UMAP-style query map labeled “Querying the human transcriptome landscape with natural language,” colored by CellWhisperer score for a text search term, with a blue-to-red color bar approximately from -10 to 10. Red and blue regions indicate transcriptomes matching or opposing the queried natural-language concepts.

Panel d shows small histogram/time-series panels of GEO submission dates for selected samples, with y-axis “Num. samples” and x-axis “GEO submission date” spanning roughly 2013 to 2023. Main visible finding: the model embeds large transcriptome collections into a searchable natural-language space, where text queries highlight biologically coherent transcriptome regions.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/result schematic for evaluating cell-type query scoring on an expert-annotated scRNA-seq dataset. Left panel shows a UMAP embedding of many colored cell clusters labeled “Expert-annotated scRNA-seq evaluation dataset (not used during training),” with an arrow pointing to a red-highlighted cluster labeled “Erythrocytes.” A “Free-text query for cell types” arrow leads to the right evaluation panel.

Right panel is labeled “Evaluation against expert-annotated cell types” and shows a query for “erythrocytes.” It contains a UMAP colored by “CellWhisperer score,” with red high-scoring cells corresponding to erythrocytes, and a density/histogram plot below with x-axis “CellWhisperer score,” y-axis “Density,” gray bars for “Other cell types,” and red bars for “Erythrocytes.” Main visible finding: erythrocytes receive distinctly higher CellWhisperer scores than other cell types for the erythrocyte text query.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel experiment result figure showing zero-shot prediction performance for common cell types. Left side has two UMAP scatter plots labeled “Tabula Sapiens annotation” and “CellWhisperer prediction,” with points colored by cell type. Right side is a heatmap/confusion-matrix-like plot titled “Tabula Sapiens (20 common cell types),” comparing expert-annotated cell classes against predicted cells, with a blue intensity legend labeled “Predicted cells per expert-annotated class (%)” from 0 to 80.

Cell types listed include erythrocyte, macrophage, monocyte, classical/non-classical monocyte, neutrophil, basophil, NK cell, CD8-positive alpha-beta T cell, CD4-positive alpha-beta memory T cell, B cell classes, capillary endothelial cell, type II pneumocyte, respiratory goblet cell, club cell, basal cell, and hepatocyte. The main visible finding is strong diagonal signal in the heatmap for many classes, indicating that CellWhisperer predictions largely match Tabula Sapiens annotations, with some off-diagonal confusion among related immune and epithelial/endothelial cell types.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure comparing a natural-language CellWhisperer single-cell RNA-seq analysis workflow with a conventional bioinformatics workflow. Panels include workflow diagrams, UMAP embeddings, query score maps, gene expression plots, chat output, differential expression ranking, and violin/box-like distributions.

Visible panels:
- **a**: CellWhisperer workflow from scRNA-seq h5ad input through automated processing to interactive exploration with AI cluster labels, cell search, and chat.
- **b**: UMAP with CellWhisperer-generated cluster labels for intestinal epithelial and immune-related cell populations.
- **c**: UMAP colored by CellWhisperer score for query “Show me stem cells.”
- **d**: Chat-style response describing a top-scoring “stem cells” subpopulation.
- **e**: UMAP showing expression of marker gene **LGR5**.
- **f**: Distribution of “stem cells” CellWhisperer score by inflammation status.
- **g**: Conventional bioinformatics workflow: integration, annotation, differential analysis, plotting.
- **h**: Raw vs integrated dataset UMAP, with legend for Healthy, Inflamed, Noninflamed.
- **i**: Cluster-level cell type annotation UMAP with labels including B cells, T cells, TA cells, colonocytes, BEST4+ epithelial, BEST2+ goblet cell.
- **j**: Cell-level annotation zoom highlighting stem cells.
- **k**: Differential expression rank plot for “Stem cells,” highlighting **LGR5** as significant.
- **l**: Stemness score distribution across cells by inflammation status, showing a significant difference.

Main visible finding: CellWhisperer appears to identify and describe stem-cell-like intestinal cell populations directly from scRNA-seq embeddings, with correspondence to known marker **LGR5** and comparison to conventional annotation/differential-expression workflows.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture diagram for a biomedical AI model. It shows paired transcriptome datasets feeding Geneformer and BioBERT encoders, producing normalized 2048-dimensional embeddings. A central matrix illustrates dot-product similarity with batch size 512 and an InfoNCE loss, including maximize/minimize regions. On the right, transcriptome-conversation paired datasets feed a Mistral 7B LLM with concatenated token embeddings for multimodal instruction tuning using cross-entropy loss on answer tokens. Labels include GEO and CELLxGENE Census data counts, Geneformer/BioBERT layer and parameter notes, frozen/unfrozen training stages, and conversation-type counts. The main visible finding is an architecture for aligning transcriptomic embeddings with language-model instruction tuning, not an experimental result plot.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Two-panel quantitative result figure from a human diseases dataset. Left panel is a grouped bar chart titled “Human Diseases dataset” showing “Recall at <top>” on the y-axis for two retrieved modalities on the x-axis: “Target” and “Transcriptomes.” Bars are grouped by recall-at-top matches 1, 5, 10, and 50, with legend in grayscale. Visible values increase with larger top-k: Target approximately 0.19, 0.55, 0.79, 0.97; Transcriptomes approximately 0.24, 0.59, 0.79, 0.98.

Right panel is a line plot titled “Human Diseases dataset” with x-axis “Epoch” and y-axis “Recall at top-5.” The curve rises from about 0.44 to around 0.58–0.62 early, then fluctuates around 0.53–0.57 across later epochs. Main finding: retrieval recall improves with larger top-k, and top-5 recall varies but remains around the mid-0.5 range after early training.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

A horizontal dot/strip plot comparing normalized scores across experimental settings for a CellWhisperer-related model. The x-axis is labeled “Normalized scores (fixed range 0-1)” from 0 to 1. The y-axis lists ablation/configuration factors including “LiT: Both models frozen,” “Loss function: JSD,” “LiT: Only language model frozen,” “LiT: Both models unfrozen,” “Batch size: 32, Grad. accum.: 16,” “Transcriptome model: scGPT,” “Data: Only GEO,” “Loss function: Mean(JSD, InfoNCE),” “Gradient accumulation: 16,” “Data: CELLxGENE Census,” “Augmentation: 2 annotation sets,” “Sample weights: Constant (1),” and “CellWhisperer embedding model.”

Colored dots show score distributions per condition, with gray horizontal bars indicating ranges or summaries. The bottom “CellWhisperer embedding model” row is highlighted in orange. Visibly, the embedding model and several ablation settings achieve mid-to-high normalized scores, while points vary broadly across metrics/configurations, with many values clustered around roughly 0.4-0.8 and some reaching near 1.0.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Bar-chart results figure with three stacked metric panels: Accuracy, F1 Score, and AUROC. The x-axis lists datasets/tasks: Tabula Sapiens, Tabula Sapiens (20 common cell types), Pancreas, ImmGen, and Asian Immune Diversity Atlas. Bars compare models from the legend: scGPT unfrozen with pseudo-bulks, scGPT frozen with pseudo-bulks and single cells, scGPT frozen with pseudo-bulks, CellWhisperer scGPT-based, and CellAssign. A side annotation groups scGPT/CellWhisperer as fine-tuned and CellAssign as zero-shot.

The figure reports cell-type or biological classification performance across datasets. Main visible finding: performance is low on Tabula Sapiens for Accuracy and F1 but high AUROC; for most other datasets AUROC is high across models, while CellWhisperer often has among the highest Accuracy/F1, especially on ImmGen and Asian Immune Diversity Atlas.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: CHATCELL facilitates single-cell analysis through conversational interactions. Black and red texts denote human and single-cell language, respectively.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Schematic workflow/diagram illustrating a biomedical AI interaction about single-cell gene expression. The panel shows chat bubbles asking for the top 100 primary genes in a randomly selected cell sorted by expression, then inferring cell type, then requesting another endothelial cell. Red gene-name lists include examples such as `GM42418`, `IL1RAPL1`, `GPHN`, `CDK8`, `LARS2`, `JARID2`, `ZC3H7A`, `FGFR2`, and others. 

There are no axes, plots, numerical scales, or legend. A stylized red blood/endothelial-like cell illustration is connected by lines to the gene-list outputs. The main point shown is that gene-expression profiles are used to identify a likely cell type, here labeled “Endothelial,” and retrieve another cell with a similar endothelial gene-expression signature.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 2: (a) Comparison of traditional single-cell analysis and CHATCELL. (b) Overview of CHATCELL.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel workflow/model schematic for a single-cell analysis foundation model called **ChatCell**.

Panel **(a)** contrasts a **traditional paradigm** with **ChatCell**. It shows a pipeline from **cell mixture** to **single-cell RNA-seq**, producing a **single-cell gene expression matrix** with genes and cells, then converting expression into a **cell sentence** through **unified sequence generation**. The traditional side shows **cell expression embedding**, **foundation model pre-training**, and **task-specific fine-tuning** for multiple tasks. ChatCell is shown performing **single-cell analysis via chat**, taking instructions and returning task-specific solutions.

Panel **(b)** shows the ChatCell construction workflow. It includes **Instruction Construction**, where a task description, input cell sentence, and target output are assembled; **Vocabulary Adaptation**, combining an original vocabulary with domain knowledge to create an expertise vocabulary and initialize the model; and a **Unified Sequence Generation for Single-cell Analysis** module. Example tasks include **random cell generation**, **pseudo-cell generation**, **cell type annotation**, and **drug sensitivity prediction**. The visible examples show gene-list “cell sentences” and generated outputs such as a likely **spinous** cell type and **resistance/drug sensitivity** response. No quantitative axes or plots are present.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 3: Performance variations in (a) random cell generation and (b) pseudo-cell generation across different expanded vocabulary sizes (in thousands).
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel experimental results figure with bar and line plots.

Panel (a) shows bar charts comparing “w/o vocabulary adaptation” vs “with vocabulary adaptation” for Cell Length, Validity (%), and Uniqueness (%). Vocabulary adaptation improves Cell Length from 97.67 to 100.00 and Validity from 97.92 to 100.00, while Uniqueness remains 100.00 for both.

Panel (b) contains four line plots versus Expanded Vocab Size (0, 7, 14, 21), with legend values K=5, K=10, K=25, K=50. Metrics are Quality (Expr.), Quality (Lev.), Discriminability (Expr.), and Discriminability (Lev.), with y-axis labeled KNN Accuracy (%). Most curves dip at expanded vocab size 7 and then increase at 14 and 21, with larger K generally producing higher accuracy.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 4: Visualization of word embeddings before and after training. A lower DB index indicates better clustering separation.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Two-panel scatter plot comparing word distributions “Before” and “After.” Legend marks blue points as “General words” and red points as “Domain-specific words.” Each panel shows unlabeled 2D coordinates with tick marks; left panel labeled “Before” has “DB Index: 99.58,” right panel labeled “After” has “DB Index: 8.00,” with an arrow between panels.

The figure appears to visualize embedding or feature-space separation of general vs domain-specific vocabulary. Main visible finding: after the transformation, domain-specific words form a more compact vertical cluster near the center, while general words remain broadly distributed, corresponding to a lower DB index.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 5: Performance (%) comparison of drug sensitivity prediction using task descriptions seen or unseen during training.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Composite experimental results figure comparing model performance on drug-sensitivity prediction tasks. The top panels show task descriptions: a training task predicts whether a cancer cell is “sensitive” or “resistant” to a drug from top 100 gene expression values in descending order, while an unseen task evaluates resistance/sensitivity to “drug” using ordered gene-expression context.

The bottom panels are horizontal bar charts with metrics on the y-axis: Recall, Precision, F1, and Acc. Legends compare “Seen task descriptions” in pink vs “Unseen task descriptions” in blue. Left plot is labeled GSE149383 with x-axis around 90-94; right plot is labeled GSE117872 with x-axis around 90-98.

Main visible finding: performance is very similar between seen and unseen task descriptions, with unseen descriptions slightly higher on several metrics, especially in GSE117872.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 6: (a) Distribution of real cells and generated cells. (b) Gene clusters and their associated pathways.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel data figure with dimensionality-reduction scatter plots of single-cell data.

(a) Shows MMD comparison between real and generated cell-source distributions. Top plot overlays “Real” and “Generated” points with MMD: 0.0077. Below are separate UMAP/t-SNE-like scatter plots labeled “Real Cells” and “Generated Cells.” Legend lists cell sources including Basal, Dermal Fibroblast, Dermal Papilla, Endothelial, Hair Shaft-cuticle.cortex, IRS, Infundibulum, Isthmus, Medulla, Mix, ORS, Spinous, TAC-1, TAC-2, ahighCD34+ bulge, and alowCD34+ bulge.

(b) Shows a clustered single-cell embedding with clusters 1-5 color-coded. Text annotations link regions of the embedding to biological functions such as immune system/inflammatory response/cell signaling processes, immune cell activation and signaling, tissue development, leukocyte functions/immune responses, and regulation of tissue structure.

Main visible finding: generated cells visually reproduce the real cell distribution and cell-source structure, while the clustered embedding is associated with distinct immune and tissue-development functional annotations.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 7: Performance (%) comparison of drug sensitivity prediction using task descriptions seen or unseen during training under base (a) and large (b) settings.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel horizontal bar chart comparing classification metrics on two datasets. Panels are labeled (a) and (b), each with subplots for GSE149383 and GSE117872. The legend compares “Seen task descriptions” in peach versus “Unseen task descriptions” in blue. Y-axis metrics are Recall, Precision, F1, and Acc; x-axes show percentage-like performance ranges around 94-99.

Main visible finding: performance is very similar for seen and unseen task descriptions across metrics. In panel (a), GSE117872 shows identical values for seen/unseen around 97.71-98.49, while GSE149383 shows slightly higher unseen values. In panel (b), seen task descriptions are generally higher than unseen, especially for GSE149383 and GSE117872.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 8: Gene pathway enrichment analysis. Genes are mapped to their corresponding biological pathways, with the significance of these associations quantified using p -values.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing PCA clustering and pathway enrichment results. The top-left panel is a PCA scatter plot titled “PCA Plots of Clusters,” with points colored by five clusters and a legend labeled Clusters 1-5. The remaining panels are horizontal bar plots for Cluster 1 through Cluster 5, each showing enriched pathways on the y-axis and `-log10(adjusted p-value)` on the x-axis.

Cluster-associated pathway labels include extracellular matrix/structure organization, renal and kidney development, leukocyte and granulocyte migration, T cell activation/differentiation, leukocyte chemotaxis/degranulation, epidermis and skin development, muscle tissue development, and epithelial cell migration. The visible finding is that the five PCA-defined clusters separate into distinct groups and show different functional enrichment profiles, with Cluster 5 having the strongest enrichment values and Cluster 1 enriched for extracellular matrix and developmental pathways.

vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing sequence-based biomedical/genomics question-answering examples paired with model performance plots.

Panels **a-f** each show a DNA/RNA/protein sequence snippet labeled `myseq.fna`, a natural-language query/answer interaction, and an evaluation plot:

- **a:** Promoter activity classification in human/mouse cells. Confusion matrix labeled “Promoters (human/mouse; MCC: 0.95)” with true vs predicted labels `No/Yes`, showing strong classification performance.
- **b:** Promoter strength regression in tobacco leaves. Scatter plot of predicted vs observed values, labeled “PCC: 0.82”.
- **c:** Mouse RNA degradation regression. Scatter plot of predicted vs observed degradation values, labeled “PCC: 0.63”.
- **d:** DNA methylation classification in HUES64 human embryonic stem cells. Confusion matrix labeled “AUROC: 0.97”, showing methylated vs non-methylated CpG prediction.
- **e:** Splice site classification across `No`, `Acceptor`, and `Donor`. Confusion matrix labeled “Splice sites (multispecies; MCC: 0.98)”, with high diagonal counts.
- **f:** Protein melting point regression for a protein CDS sequence. Scatter plot of predicted vs observed melting point values, labeled “PCC: 0.89”.

Main visible finding: the model appears to answer biological sequence questions and achieve high performance across promoter prediction, methylation, splice-site classification, RNA degradation, promoter strength, and protein melting point tasks.

Multi-panel performance comparison figure with data plots. Panel **a** is a grouped bar chart across genomics, RNA, and protein tasks, with y-axis **Metric** from 0 to 1 and many task labels on the x-axis, including histone marks, DNA methylation, chromatin accessibility, promoters, splice sites, lncRNA, enhancer/promoter strength, RNA degradation/polyadenylation, protein fluorescence, stability, and meltome. The legend compares baseline models such as **AgroNT, NT, DeepSTARR, ChromTransfer, ESM2, DNABERT, APARENT2, Saluki** against **ChatNT**.

Panels **b-d** are violin/box-style summaries comparing **Baselines** vs **ChatNT**: across all 27 tasks, 17 classification tasks, and 10 regression tasks. The main visible finding is that ChatNT achieves broadly comparable performance to task-specific baselines across many genomics/RNA/protein benchmarks, with similar distributions in the summary panels.

vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing a genomics model workflow and benchmark results.

Panel a is a workflow/model architecture diagram for deriving perplexity-based probabilities: DNA sequence input is passed through a DNA encoder and DNA resampler, then queried through an English language model using prompts such as “Can you find a promoter in this DNA sequence @myseq.fna?” Perplexity calculations produce logits for negative and positive answers.

Panel b is a calibration plot for chromatin accessibility in HepG2, with x-axis “Mean predicted probability” and y-axis “Fraction of positives.” It compares a dashed “Perfectly calibrated” line, teal initial perplexity-based probabilities, and blue calibrated probabilities.

Panels c and d are histograms of predicted probabilities before and after calibration. Panel c shows initial perplexity-based probabilities concentrated mostly around mid-range values; panel d shows calibrated probabilities shifted toward extremes near 0 and near 0.8-1.0.

Panel e is a horizontal bar chart of binary classification tasks, plotting MCC on the x-axis from 0 to 1. It compares ChatNT answer versus ChatNT perplexity across genomic tasks including histone marks, DNA methylation, chromatin accessibility, promoters, enhancers, splice donors/acceptors, and lncRNAs. The visible finding is that performance varies by task, with high MCC for promoter, splice donor, and splice acceptor tasks, and lower values for some histone modification and enhancer tasks.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure combining a model workflow schematic and quantitative sequence-motif plots.

Panel a shows “Interpretation of ChatNT predictions”: token attribution/gradient-based interpretation for a DNA sequence passed through a DNA encoder, DNA resampler, and English language model. Labels include “Token attributions,” “Gradients × Input,” “Gradient of answer w.r.t. DNA sequence,” and an example prompt asking whether a sequence contains a TATA promoter. A sequence-logo-style attribution heatmap is shown below.

Panels b-d show motif and k-mer attribution/frequency results:
- b: “Splice donors,” with a sequence logo enriched around a GT donor motif and a bar/stem plot of top k-mers per sequence.
- c: “Splice acceptors,” with a sequence logo showing enrichment near an AG acceptor motif and a corresponding k-mer frequency plot.
- d: “TATA promoters,” with a sequence logo showing a TATA-like promoter motif and k-mer frequency plot.

Axes include k-mer on the x-axis and “Frequency among top-k-mers per sequence” on the y-axis. A legend distinguishes “Yes” token and “No” token colors. Main visible finding: gradient/token attribution recovers biologically recognizable motifs for splice donor, splice acceptor, and TATA promoter prediction tasks.

figure_candidates.caption: Fig. 1 | Chroma is a generative model for proteins and protein complexes that combines structured diffusion for protein backbones with scalable molecular neural networks for backbone synthesis and all-atom design. a , A correlated diffusion process with chain and radius-of-gyration constraints gradually transforms protein structures into random collapsed polymers (right to left). The reverse process (left to right) can be expressed in terms of a time-dependent optimal denoiser ̂ t ( , ) θ t x x that maps noisy coordinates x t at time t to predicted denoised coordinates 0 x . b , We parameterize this in terms
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel workflow/model architecture figure for protein complex design using polymer diffusion.

Panel a shows a diffusion trajectory from a “collapsed polymer system” through noisy intermediate structures \(x_t\) to a “protein complex backbone” \(x_0\), followed by a “design network” producing an “all-atom complex.” Arrows label generation as reverse polymer diffusion and training as forward polymer diffusion.

Panel b illustrates denoising: a noisy structure \(x_t\) is processed by a random graph neural network with \(O(N)\) or \(O(N\log N)\) edges, producing confidence-weighted predicted inter-residue geometries, then an equivariant geometry solver outputs a predicted denoised structure \(\hat{x}_\theta(x_t,t)\).

Panel c is a probabilistic conditioning schematic showing a time-dependent prior \(\log[p_t(x)]\) plus time-dependent conditioners \(\log[p_\theta(y|x)]\) forming a time-dependent posterior \(\log[p_t(x|y)]\). Legend items include symmetry, substructure, shape, and semantics.

Main visible message: the method generates protein complex backbones by denoising collapsed/noisy polymer structures under optional structural or semantic conditioning, then converts the backbone to an all-atom protein complex.

vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure combining plots, schematic workflows, and model architecture.

- **Panel a:** Bar chart of **token composition (%)** comparing **Group A sparse-low windows** and **Group B dense-low windows**. Categories include interchangeable expressions, common vocabulary, biomedical entities, and causal/reasoning chains. Group A appears enriched for interchangeable/common vocabulary tokens, while Group B appears enriched for biomedical entities and causal/reasoning chains.
- **Panel b:** Line/trace plot of **4096-token response confidence**, with highlighted windows: **Window A sparse low-confidence** and **Window B dense low-confidence**. Zoom-in plots show token confidence patterns in each window, with local mean confidence annotated.
- **Panel c:** Workflow schematic for **Balanced Fine-Tuning (BFT)**. It contrasts token-level weighting for sparse low-confidence tokens in Group A with sample-level or trajectory-level weighting for dense low-confidence Group B, aiming to stabilize gradients and reduce overfitting.
- **Panel d:** Model pipeline diagram: an **LLM** plus **biomedical trajectory** undergoes **BFT** to produce **LLM-BFT**, which generates descriptions of biomedical entities and maps them through a text embedding model into an embedding space.

Main visible finding: low-confidence token regions are separated into sparse and dense patterns, with different token compositions, and the proposed BFT strategy weights them differently to improve biomedical entity description/embedding behavior.

Legends show cell types including BCell, EC, Fibroblast, MSC, Mastcell, MonoMaphDC, NK, Plasma, SMC1, SMC2, Tcell, and Unknown; patient IDs including affected and control samples; and phenotypes including **Ascending only**, **Ascending to descending**, **Ascending w/ root**, and **Control**.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel UMAP embedding comparison figure from a single-cell multi-omics integration experiment. The grid has 4 rows labeled `BFT`, `BBKNN`, `Harmony`, and `scMODAL`, and 3 columns colored by `modality`, `celltype`, and `donor`.

Each panel shows a 2D UMAP plot with axes `UMAP1` and `UMAP2`. Legends indicate modality labels `ADT` and `RNA`; cell types including `B`, `CD4 T`, `CD8 T`, `DC`, `Mono`, `NK`, `other`, and `other T`; and donors `P1` through `P8`.

The figure compares how different integration methods mix modalities and donors while preserving cell-type structure. Visibly, `scMODAL` and `BFT` show stronger overlap between ADT and RNA modalities than `BBKNN` or `Harmony`, while cell-type clusters remain distinguishable across methods.

figure_candidates.caption: Fig. 1 (A) The schematic overview of the OKR-CELL method. (B) The illustration of several downstream tasks implemented via OKR-CELL, including cell clustering, batch affect correlation, cell-type annotation and cross-modal retrieval.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel workflow/model architecture figure labeled **A** and **B**. Panel **A** shows a cross-modal cell-text pretraining pipeline: scRNA-seq/cell omics data and cell description text are tokenized, passed through **Cell Encoder** and **Text Encoder**, aligned by **cross-modal similarity**, and trained with intra-modal cellular generative pretraining plus cross-modal cell-text pretraining. It also includes a retrieval-augmented LLM workflow with **Retriever**, **Database**, **LLM**, and **Reliability Screen** for generating cell type definitions.

Panel **B** shows downstream application of a **pretrained cell encoder** from scRNA-seq/gene expression tokens. Outputs are shown as small UMAP-like embeddings and task panels labeled **Clustering**, **Batch-effect Correction**, **Cell Type Annotation**, **Zero-shot Annotation**, **Few-shot Annotation**, and **Cross-modal Retrieval**.

No conventional numeric axes are visible. The figure primarily depicts a multimodal single-cell foundation model workflow linking gene expression profiles with text descriptions for cell representation learning, annotation, retrieval, and downstream analysis.

(B) Bar plot of AvgBIO scores across four datasets (blood, kidney, hPancreas and hpbmc). (C) T-SNE plots of cell embeddings generated by different methods on blood and hPancreas datasets. (D) Bar plot of AvgBIO and AvgBatch scores of batch effect correction by different methods on hPancreas dataset. (E) Bar plot of AvgBIO and AvgBatch scores of batch effect correction by different methods on hpbmc reference dataset. vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel benchmarking figure comparing single-cell foundation/model methods across datasets.

Panels:
- **A**: Bubble/table-style summary for datasets **Blood**, **Kidney**, and **Hpancreas**, with metrics **ARI** and **AMI** across methods **Geneformer**, **scBERT**, **scFoundation**, **scGPT**, and **OKR-CELL**. Larger/darker bubbles indicate higher values; OKR-CELL appears highest in most rows.
- **B**: Bar chart labeled **AvgBIO**, comparing methods across **blood**, **kidney**, **hpancreas**, and **hpbmc**. OKR-CELL generally has the tallest bars.
- **C**: UMAP/t-SNE-like embedding panels for **blood** and **hpancreas**, shown for each method, with colored cell clusters.
- **D** and **E**: Bar charts for **AvgBIO** and **AvgBatch**, again comparing the same methods; OKR-CELL is visibly among the top performers.
- **F**: Radar/spider plot comparing metrics including **Isolated labels**, **KMeans NMI**, **KMeans ARI**, **Silhouette label**, **cLISI**, **Silhouette batch**, **Graph connectivity**, and **PCR comparison**. OKR-CELL has the largest overall polygon in several biological clustering metrics.

Main visible finding: **OKR-CELL** appears to outperform or match competing methods across clustering agreement and biological conservation metrics while maintaining competitive batch-related scores.

(C) Bar plot of accuracy and f1-score for cell type annotation by different methods on small-intestine, spleen and hpbmc reference datasets. (D) Bar plot of accuracy and f1-score for few-shot cell type annotation different methods on zheng68k and Great-Apes reference datasets. (E) Bar plot of accuracy and f1-score for zero-shot cell type annotation different methods on eye, prostate-gland and GreatApes reference datasets. (F) Sankey diagram visualizes the correspondence between predicted labels and reference annotations for zero-shot cell type annotation by LangCell and OKR-CELL methods on prostate-gland reference dataset.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel benchmarking figure for cell-type annotation across tissues/datasets.

Figure type: UMAP/scatter embeddings, confusion matrices, bar plots, and Sankey/alluvial classification maps.

Visible panels:
- **A**: UMAP-style cell embeddings for **eye**, **hPBMC**, and **small_intestine**, comparing models including **Geneformer**, **scBERT**, **scFoundation**, **scGPT**, and **OKR-CELL**. Each plot is colored by **cell type**, with legends listing tissue-specific cell populations. Titles report **AvgBIO** scores.
- **B**: Confusion matrices for **Kidney** and **Small intestine**, comparing predicted vs. true cell-type labels.
- **C**: Bar plots of **Accuracy** and **F1-score** across datasets including **small_intestine**, **spleen**, and **hPBMC**, comparing multiple models.
- **D**: Bar plots comparing **zero-shot** and related settings for accuracy across methods including **LangCell**, **scCUPNET**, and **OKR-CELL**.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: BIOREASON Architecture. Schematic representation of our novel multimodal framework that integrates a DNA foundation model with a Large Language Model.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture diagram for a genomics-language model system. It shows DNA sequences passed through a frozen Evo2-1B model, then a learnable linear projection aligning Evo2 embeddings to Qwen3 dimensions. These projected DNA embeddings are stacked with tokenized text embeddings from a BioReason chat template and Qwen3 tokenizer, using special DNA pad/start/end tokens and a Qwen3 embedding matrix. The combined embeddings feed into a Qwen3-4B model.

Visible labels include “Stacked DNA and Text Embeddings,” “Frozen Evo2-1B,” “Learnable Linear Projection,” “Qwen3 Tokenizer,” “Qwen3 Embedding Matrix,” “BioReason Chat Template,” “Question,” and “Response (with reasoning).” The example biomedical prompt concerns chromosome 12, pathway definition involving LRRK2, CYCS, APAF1, CASP9, and CASP3, and asks about the biological effect of an LRRK2 allele. The response panel gives chain-of-thought-style tags and concludes “Parkinson’s disease.”

Main visible point: the figure illustrates a multimodal architecture combining DNA sequence embeddings with biomedical text prompts to generate disease-related reasoning responses.

vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific workflow and dataset summary figure for a biomedical question-answering/reasoning dataset built from KEGG variant networks and disease annotations.

Panels:
- **A**: Schematic of a KEGG variant network-to-disease example. Shows pathway, gene names, associated disease, and a ground-truth literature statement. Example involves **LRRK2**, pathway **LRRK2 -> CYCS -> APAF1 -> CASP9 -> CASP3**, and **Parkinson’s Disease**.
- **B**: Example question-answer pair and reasoning trace. The question includes a variant sequence and chromosome number, network definition, genes, and asks for the biological effect/disease. The reasoning trace identifies a **C-to-G substitution**, links it to an LRRK2 gain-of-function mutation, and concludes **Parkinson’s Disease**.
- **C**: Workflow diagram showing three task pipelines: KEGG pathway, coding variants, and coding non-SNVs. Data sources include KEGG, ClinVar, dbSNP, OMIM, COSMIC, and GPT-4o formatting. Outputs include **1,449 QA pairs**, **60,810 QA pairs**, and **36,088 QA pairs**.
- **D**: Stacked bar chart showing train/validation/test split percentages for KEGG, Task 2, and Task 3 QA pairs. Most data are train/validation, with smaller test sets labeled **290**, **1,233**, and **873**.
- **E**: Stacked bar chart showing disease-category composition across KEGG, Task 2, and Task 3. Legend includes benign, cardiovascular, immunological, metabolic, musculoskeletal, neurological, oncological, other, and sensory disorder categories.

Main visible finding: the figure presents construction of a variant-network biomedical reasoning QA benchmark, with thousands of generated QA pairs spanning multiple variant tasks and disease categories.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 3: Case Study of BIOREASON's Output
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Three-panel schematic/table-style figure comparing a biomedical QA example across **Question**, **Ground Truth (KEGG)**, and **BioReason’s Output**.

Figure type: workflow/evaluation example for biomedical reasoning or question answering.

Visible labels/panels: left vertical label “KEGG Data Point”; panels titled “Question,” “Ground Truth (KEGG),” and “BioReason’s Output.”

Content shown: the question asks about chromosome 17, pathway “Actin,” genes including **PFN1/profilin 1**, and a **PFN1 allele**, asking for the biological effect and associated disease. The ground truth traces KEGG reasoning from a **C>T mutation in PFN1** to altered actin dynamics, axonal transport defects, motor neuron degeneration, and **Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)**. BioReason’s output gives similar reasoning and answers **amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)**.

Main visible finding: the model output matches the KEGG-derived ground truth that a PFN1 mutation is linked to ALS through disruption of profilin-1 function and actin cytoskeleton dynamics.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 4: Mean reward progression during GRPO training across different BioReason model configurations over 1000 training steps. Shaded regions represent per-step reward variance across the batch of 8 generations per query.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Line plot of training/validation loss over global training steps. The x-axis is labeled `train/global_step`; the y-axis shows loss values roughly from 1.0 to 2.7. A legend at the top lists multiple model variants/runs, including OpenAI CLIP ViT variants. Several colored curves with noisy vertical traces are shown, with smoothed lines increasing and then plateauing. The main visible finding is that different runs converge to similar high loss values around ~2.6-2.7, while one orange/brown run starts much lower and rises more gradually, remaining below the others for most of training.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure  1.  Overview  of  the  GEMGen  framework.  a, Conceptual  illustration  of GEMGen. Given transcriptomic profiles describing transitions  between  healthy  and diseased  cellular  states,  GEMGen  generates  candidate  compounds  predicted  to induce the desired  phenotypic  change. b, End-to-end  workflow  of  GEMGen. Transcriptomic  changes  are  provided  as  text-based, rank-ordered  lists  of  up-  and down-regulated genes within a specific cellular context. GEMGen generates candidate compounds in SMILES format, which are optionally filtered by additional modules and ranked using the GEMGen scorer to prioritize candidates for experimental validation and downstream development. c , Model architecture and training strategy. GEMGen builds  on  a  scientific  foundation  model  (e.g.,  NatureLM)  adapted  from  a  generalpurpose  large  language  model  (e.g.,  GPT-5).  On  this  basis,  GEMGen  performs bioentity representation generation, followed by phenotype-guided compound generation  and  compound-phenotype  matching. d ,  Transformation  of  quantitative transcriptomic measurements into standardized, text-based features. Multi-panel scientific schematic and results figure describing **GEMGen**, a generative model for compound design guided by cell-state gene expression phenotypes.

Panels include:
- **a:** Concept diagram showing compounds shifting a diseased cell-state landscape toward healthy.
- **b:** Workflow from an instruction prompt specifying cell type and up/down gene lists, through GEMGen generation, SMILES outputs, filtering, matching score, and experimental/clinical validation.
- **c:** Model architecture schematic: general-purpose language model adapted to scientific foundation model, with modules for bioentity representation generation, phenotype-guided compound generation, and compound-phenotype matching.
- **d:** Feature extraction workflow from transcriptomes to differentially expressed genes and ranked DEG lists, with labels for quantitative feature levels and robustness.
- **e:** Two density plots comparing cosine similarity distributions for random pairs vs duplications: DEG fold changes and DEG embeddings, with W-distance values shown.
- **f:** Training/evaluation setup listing L1000 compound-phenotype pairs, held-out compounds, single-cell chemical perturbations, genetic perturbation, and cell-state transition.

Main visible finding: the figure presents GEMGen as a phenotype-guided compound generation framework using DEG-based cell-state representations, with embedding-based DEG features appearing more robustly separated for duplicated profiles than raw fold-change features.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing evaluation of a generative molecular model, GEMGen, on novel compound and novel condition test sets.

Figure type: workflow schematic, UMAP/scatter embedding, density plot, cumulative distribution plots, bar charts, boxplots, heatmaps, and molecular structure examples.

Visible panels and labels:
- Panels `a-b`: test-set construction and filtering workflow. Novel compound test set curated from L1000 with 404 samples; novel condition test set curated from Tahoe-100M with 640 samples. Generated molecules pass syntactic validity check and de-duplication.
- Panel `c`: UMAP plot comparing ChemDiv, Train, and Generated molecules.
- Panel `d`: density plot of syntactic validity ratio for GEMGen checkpoints 1-3.
- Panel `e`: cumulative distributions of similarity to ground-truth molecules for GEMGen checkpoints, merged GEMGen, GexMolGen, VAE-based, GPT-5, and ChemDiv.
- Panels `f-g`: L1000 novel compound set results, showing number of samples with possible hits and hits per input sample.
- Panel `h`: heatmap of hit counts per input sample for GEMGen checkpoints and merge.
- Panels `i` and `m`: example prompts with cell line/gene expression conditions, ground-truth molecules, and generated hit molecules with similarity color scale.
- Panels `j-k-l`: Tahoe-100M novel condition set results with bar chart, boxplot, and hit-count heatmap.

Biological/model quantity shown: molecule generation quality and retrieval-like hit performance under transcriptomic/cellular perturbation conditions, measured by syntactic validity, similarity to ground-truth molecules, and number of possible hits per sample.

Main visible finding: GEMGen, especially the merged model, produces more possible hits than comparison methods across both test sets, while generated molecules overlap broadly with train/ChemDiv chemical space and include examples similar to known ground-truth compounds such as nilotinib and dinaciclib.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure  3.  Scoring  model  distinguishes  true  compound-phenotype  pairs  and prioritizes effective candidates. a-b , Performance of the scorer in distinguishing true compound-phenotype pairs from random negatives, evaluated by (a) precision-recall and  (b)  receiver  operating  characteristic  (ROC)  curves. c ,  Distribution  of  scores assigned to positive and negative pairs. The scorer assigns significantly higher values to true pairs (two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, P < 1×10 -15 ). N=2,088 for both positive and negative pairs. d , Precision at different score threshold. Dashed line: a precision of  0.950  is  achieved  at  a  threshold  of  0.8. e, Score  distributions  for  compounds generated in the L1000 (top) and Tahoe-100M (bottom) test sets. 'Hits' are generated molecules  with  Tanimoto  similarity  >0.6  to  ground-truth  compounds;  'non-hits'  are dissimilar molecules. The scorer assigns higher scores to hits than to non-hits. f, Score distributions for generated compounds versus randomly shuffled compounds in the L1000  novel  compound  and  Tahoe-100M  novel  condition  test  sets. Pvalues  are calculated with two-sides Mann-Whitney U test. g , Effect of filtering by score threshold on candidate retention and hit rate in the L1000 (top, N=203) and Tahoe-100M (bottom, N=242) test sets. Shaded bands: 95% confidence intervals.
