routes.route_label: gene expression profiles for transcriptome-to-language generation
routes.evidence_quote: Transcriptome-to-language generation was evaluated on a held-out validation split of the gene-text paired dataset that was not used for model training. Each model was prompted with transcriptomic input to generate a biological description, which was compared with the corresponding transcriptome-grounded reference description using three complementary metrics. BLEU-4 measures local n-gram precision between generated and reference texts [30]. ROUGE-L evaluates sequence-level structural overlap based on the longest common subsequence [31]. BERTScore F1 computes contextual semantic similarity between generated and reference descriptions in embedding space [32].

routes.route_label: H&E images for spatial gene expression prediction
routes.evidence_quote: To evaluate whether histology-derived representations retained molecular information, we trained a lightweight regression head on top of SciCore-Omics visual embeddings to predict spot-level gene expression from H&E image patches. Experiments were conducted on the normal human heart spatial transcriptomics dataset comprising 39 sections. To avoid information leakage caused by spatial correlations between neighbouring spots within the same tissue section, we used section-level 10-fold crossvalidation. Specifically, the 39 sections were partitioned into 10 folds at the section level. In each fold, the model was trained only on spots from the training sections and tested on spots from the held-out section or sections. The prediction targets were the top 50 genes with the highest expression in the training set, and performance was evaluated on the held-out spots from the test sections. Before training and evaluation, all spots were subjected to quality-control filtering, retaining only spots with at least 500 detected genes.
routes.section_heading: 3.8 Spatial gene expression prediction from histology

routes.route_label: histological image patches for embedding-based spatial domain recognition
routes.evidence_quote: We evaluated SciCore-Omics in both embedding-based and generative settings. For embedding-based evaluation, frozen model embeddings were extracted from image-only, gene-only or joint image-gene input and passed to a lightweight classification head. Performance was assessed using macro-F1 to account for class imbalance across spatial domains.
routes.section_heading: 3.9 Spatial domain, pathway and marker-gene evaluation

routes.route_label: histological image patches for generative spatial domain recognition
routes.evidence_quote: Another important task in spatial transcriptomics analysis is spatial domain identification [34-36]. We assessed SciCore-Omics in two settings. First, we examined whether the embeddings learned by the model encode spatial domain information by training a classification head on a frozen model to predict spatial domain labels. Second, we assessed whether the model can generate natural language descriptions containing spatial domain-related information. We defined the task as follows: for each spot, SciCoreOmics takes histological image patches and/or gene expression profiles as input to generate biological descriptions from which region labels, pathway labels, and marker genes are extracted (Fig. 4a). We conducted evaluations on a spatial transcriptomics dataset of the human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) [37]. This dataset comprises 12 tissue sections with paired H&E images and spatial gene expression data generated by the 10x Genomics Visium platform, along with manual cortical layer annotations.

routes.route_label: candidate class names for zero-shot histopathological classification
routes.evidence_quote: We evaluated zero-shot histopathology classification on four public H&E benchmarks: MHIST, BACH, NCT-CRC-HE-100K and PatchCamelyon. For each image, the model was given a dataset-specific closed set of candidate class names and instructed to return exactly one class label. No task-specific fine-tuning, parameter updates or in-context examples were used.
routes.section_heading: 1.5 SciCore-Omics supports zero-shot tissue-level histopathology classification

routes.evidence_quote: image-question-answer triples

Pathology visual question answering was evaluated on PathVQA, which contains approximately 4,998 pathology images and 32,795 image-question-answer pairs [44]. Evaluation followed the standard separation between open-ended and closed-ended questions. In the fine-tuned setting, the model was trained using image-question-answer triples and evaluated using benchmark-standard answer matching. Closedended questions were scored after normalizing yes/no outputs. For open-ended questions, both predictions and reference answers were normalized. Performance was reported as token-level recall, defined as the fraction of reference tokens appearing in the prediction, with multiset matching.

routes.route_label: whole-slide H&E images for H&E-based pathology reasoning
routes.evidence_quote: We next examined whether the model could extend this capability to a more clinically oriented caselevel reasoning setting. In this evaluation, only the whole-slide H&E images were used as the model input, while immunohistochemistry and pathology reports were withheld from the model and referenced solely for expert assessment (Fig. 6b). The inference workflow was designed to simulate a staged pathological review process. First, SciCore-Omics reviewed the low-magnification overview of the whole-slide image to identify tumour-rich regions and representative tumour-stroma structures. Second, representative tumour patches were selected from these regions for high-magnification assessment, with attention to interpretable morphological features, including tumour cell density, nuclear atypia, hyperchromasia, suspected mitotic activity, necrosis and stromal reaction. Finally, the model integrated evidence across multiple regions to generate a case-level interpretation of the proliferative status.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing a multimodal single-cell foundation model overview and dataset/task summaries.

Panel a is a concentric donut/ring chart summarizing dataset coverage by modality, species, age group, brain region, and disease, with legends for categories such as epigenomics, transcriptomics, spatial transcriptomics; mouse, marmoset, macaque, human; prenatal to aged; cortical and other brain regions; and disease/normal classes.

Panel b contains word-cloud summaries for metadata fields labeled Question Type, Class, Subclass, Region, Age group, and Disease, highlighting terms such as GABA, GL, oligo, Astro, region names, age values, Alzheimer, Normal, disease, and glioma.

Panel c is a model/workflow architecture diagram. Cell and feature inputs from multi-omics and multi-species data are tokenized, passed through a gene encoder, projected with graph convolutional networks and cross-attention, then connected to a large language model with text input/output. Six example task panels are shown: cell type annotation, cell origin prediction, aging clock, disease status inference, gene mask prediction, and spatial mask prediction.

Panel d shows a two-stage training strategy: Stage 1 freezes the gene encoder and LLM while training the projector; Stage 2 trains the gene encoder, projector, and LLM with LoRA.

Main visible finding: the figure presents a unified architecture and training workflow for connecting single-cell/multi-omics biological features to LLM-based question answering across annotation, species/origin, aging, disease, and masked prediction tasks.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: Token analysis, BFT, and applications. a : Semantic composition of low-confidence tokens inside Group A (sparse-low) and Group B (dense-low). b : 4096-token trace illustrating one sparse-low window (Group A) and one dense-low window (Group B). c : BFT applies token- and sample-level loss adjustments. d : BFT-generated biomedical profiles are encoded by a text embedding model for downstream representation tasks.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure combining plots, schematic workflows, and model architecture.

- **Panel a:** Bar chart of **token composition (%)** comparing **Group A sparse-low windows** and **Group B dense-low windows**. Categories include interchangeable expressions, common vocabulary, biomedical entities, and causal/reasoning chains. Group A appears enriched for interchangeable/common vocabulary tokens, while Group B appears enriched for biomedical entities and causal/reasoning chains.
- **Panel b:** Line/trace plot of **4096-token response confidence**, with highlighted windows: **Window A sparse low-confidence** and **Window B dense low-confidence**. Zoom-in plots show token confidence patterns in each window, with local mean confidence annotated.
- **Panel c:** Workflow schematic for **Balanced Fine-Tuning (BFT)**. It contrasts token-level weighting for sparse low-confidence tokens in Group A with sample-level or trajectory-level weighting for dense low-confidence Group B, aiming to stabilize gradients and reduce overfitting.
- **Panel d:** Model pipeline diagram: an **LLM** plus **biomedical trajectory** undergoes **BFT** to produce **LLM-BFT**, which generates descriptions of biomedical entities and maps them through a text embedding model into an embedding space.

Main visible finding: low-confidence token regions are separated into sparse and dense patterns, with different token compositions, and the proposed BFT strategy weights them differently to improve biomedical entity description/embedding behavior.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 6: Workflow for extracting biological embeddings from LLM-BFT. a : LLM-BFT generates profile texts for entities of interest (e.g., a specific gene). The gene profile text is encoded by OpenAI TEXT-EMBEDDING-ADA-002 (the same text encoder GenePT uses) to obtain gene embeddings, so that GenePT (GPT-4o + ada-002) and LLM-BFT (BFT-70B + ada-002) differ only in the LLM that produces the profile text. b : For a single-cell dataset, gene embeddings are weighted by gene expression values to generate cell embeddings.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture schematic with two labeled panels, **a** and **b**. Panel **a** shows an LLM-based gene text embedding pipeline: a user prompt (“Tell me about gene.”) is processed by **LLM-BFT**, producing an LLM response with gene name/function/interaction text; texts for gene x through gene y are converted via **Text to embedding** into a **gene embedding (N, 2048)** matrix. Panel **b** shows a cell-by-gene expression matrix for **M cells** and **N genes** multiplied by the **gene embedding (N, 2048)** matrix to produce a **cell embedding (M, 2048)** matrix. Main visible message: gene-level text embeddings are derived from LLM responses and combined with gene expression data to generate cell embeddings.

figure_candidates.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of Shusi. a, Pipeline for constructing single-cell protein interaction networks from scRNA-seq data. b, Architecture of the Shusi model for predicting novel interactions on single cell level. d, Fine-tuning and application of Shusi to AML patient scRNA-seq data.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel workflow/model architecture figure with panels labeled **a**, **b**, and **c**.

Panel **a** shows **data collection and preprocessing** for **scRNA-seq** and protein/network data: “23 cancer types, 234 cell lines,” “12,350 proteins,” an experimentally validated **STRING-E** network, a t-SNE-like scRNA-seq plot, and construction of **75,010 networks**.

Panel **b** shows **model training**: a **large language model** encodes amino acid sequences and functional descriptions into protein embeddings, then a **variational graph autoencoder** with a **GIN encoder**, latent variable **Z**, and decoder performs graph isomorphism/network link prediction for cell-specific networks.

Panel **c** shows **drug target identification** using a “Shushi Model,” fine-tuning on **AML patient scRNA-seq**, link prediction, target identification, and experimental validation.

Main visible finding/message: the figure presents an end-to-end computational pipeline connecting cancer scRNA-seq, protein language-model embeddings, graph neural network link prediction, and drug target discovery/validation.

Multi-panel scientific figure combining dataset summaries, model workflow diagrams, ablation studies, and biological network validation results. Panels are labeled a-o.

Figure type: bar charts, boxplots, scatter/point plots, workflow schematics, network diagrams, histograms, and violin plots.

Visible content:
- Panel a summarizes tissues with axes for `#Cell lines`, `#Cells in Each Cell lines`, `#Genes`, and `#Edges`.
- Panels b-c compare deep learning models such as GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE, GATv2, VoAE, and Shusi, with metrics including `#Parameters (M)` and `Precision`.
- Panel d shows a model architecture/workflow using amino acid sequence and functional description embeddings, including Galactica, Sentence-BERT, and feature fusion.
- Panels e and g show ablation studies of feature embeddings with `Top 1000 Precision (%)`.
- Panel f illustrates edge scoring with and without expression information.
- Panels h-m show predicted and experimental biological networks for cell lines, with validation score annotations.
- Panels k-l show histograms of validation scores for MCF7 10X and MDAMB231 BGI.

figure_candidates.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the TISSUENARRATOR framework. A. TISSUENARRATOR takes as input a tissue patch, encodes individual cells into cell sentences, and assembles a spatial sentence from neighboring cells. The spatial sentence can be interpreted by an LLM with biological prior knowledge and contextual understanding to predict gene expressions in a cell and to answer questions about tissues. Text output of the LLM can be further transformed into gene expression levels. B. TISSUENARRATOR supports four downstream tasks: cell generation, neighborhood perturbation, genetic perturbation, and conversational tissue querying. For cell generation tasks, model-generated cell sentences can be converted back into gene expression space.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model schematic with two labeled panels, **A** and **B**. Panel A shows a tissue patch converted into “cell sentences” with ordered gene lists, then into a “spatial sentence” containing ordered cells with position, metadata, cell type, and gene list. An LLM with biological prior knowledge/contextual understanding is used for generative prediction, including cell prediction and text prediction, and quantitative prediction of gene expression values for genes such as G1, G2, G3. Panel B lists applications: cell generation, conversational tissue querying, genetic perturbation, and neighborhood perturbation. No numerical experimental data or axes are shown; the main content is a conceptual architecture/workflow for spatial tissue modeling with language-model-style representations.

figure_candidates.caption: Fig. 2 X-Atlas/Pisces enables identification of context-dependent and context-independent perturbations. (A) Distribution of median UMIs per cell (top), median genes per cell (middle), and median on-target KD % (bottom) across GEMs for each screen in X-Atlas/Pisces. Black lines indicate median. (B) Recall of annotated gene pairs from CORUM (left) and STRING (right), calculated across all possible subsets of 1-7 screens. Error bars represent standard deviation across subsets. (C) Schematic of binary classifier for classifying perturbed cells from non-targeting controls (NTCs) (left). Input is a balanced mixture of perturbed cells for a given perturbation and NTCs. Model is logistic regression with L1-penalization (LASSO). Outputs are significance of the perturbation as measured by a one-sided binomial test and the features (genes) used to make the prediction. Percentage of perturbed cells with a significant phenotype (FDR < 0.05) as measured by a LASSO binary classifier (right). (D) Heatmap of F1 scores for perturbations in X-Atlas/Pisces clustered based on F1 scores across screens. Rows represent perturbations (n=6,412) that pass the following filtering criteria: (1) present in ≥ 3 screens, (2) ≥ 10 cells in each screen the perturbation was present in, (3) significant phenotype (FDR < 0.05) in at least 1 screen, and (4) F1 score ≥ 0.75 in at least 1 screen. Grey represents absence of a perturbation in that screen. Columns represent screens that are hierarchically clustered by similarity in F1 scores (colorbar). (E) Mean F1 score versus mean Jaccard index for perturbations across screens. Points are colored by F1 score coefficient of variation (CV) (colorbar). (F) UMAP of significant perturbations with at least one non-self feature (n=35,016) colored by screen. Clusters are labeled with CORUM complex enrichments, colored black if ≤ 50% of perturbations are from any individual screen, or the majority screen color otherwise. Inset structures of representative protein complexes are color-coded by whether the protein is targeted by a genetic perturbation in the indicated clusters (green shades are present, gray is absent).

figure_candidates.caption: Fig. 3 X-Cell achieves robust generalization across cellular contexts and perturbation benchmarks through diffusion pre-training. (A) X-Cell, initialized with scGPT encoder weights, was continually pre-trained on the XAtlas/Pisces perturbation corpus across four screens (HCT116, HEK293T, HepG2, and iPSC), using over 10 million cells and 37K perturbation-context combinations for training and evaluation. Radar plots summarize the relative ranking of the four benchmark models. (D) Prior knowledge attribution on Replogle-Nadig test perturbations. Pie chart shows average attention weights from X-Cell's final cross-attention layer. Line plot shows the performance drop on six metrics after randomizing embeddings from each knowledge source. figure_candidates.caption: Supplementary Figure 7 Architecture ablations, training efficiency, and scaling analysis for X-Cell-Ultra. (A) Architecture and loss ablation on the 4.9B model (Replogle-Nadig, 6 epochs). Scatter shows δ -norm ratio ˆ ρ vs. DE Pearson r for six configurations; color = MAE. The red shaded region (ˆ ρ < 0 . 2) indicates conservative collapse (predicting small effects). Replacing scale-invariant losses with CCC and removing the hidden residual shortcut progressively recovered both magnitude (ˆ ρ : 0 . 22 → 0 . 51) and direction (DEr : 0 . 05 → 0 . 33); see Table A1. (B) Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) comparison. X-Cell-Ultra achieves 41% MFU on 64 H200 GPUs, comparable to Llama 3 (reported 38-43% [95]) and ∼ 20 × the 55M X-Cell (2%). (C) Normalized loss scaling (relative to 83M model). Both train (dashed, α = 0 . 32, R 2 = 0 . 96) and test (solid, α = 0 . 03, R 2 = 0 . 97) follow power laws; color = DE Pearson r . (D) Individual validation metrics vs. trainable parameters: centroid accuracy (left) and per-perturbation MAE (right), colored by validation loss. (E) Training dynamics over 20 epochs: test loss (left) and DE Pearson r (right) for all five model sizes.

- **A:** Dataset/screen overview. Shows X-Atlas datasets **Pisces (25.6M)** and **Orion (8M)** across screens including **HCT116, HEK293T, HepG2, iPSC, Jurkat resting/active, and iPSC Multi-Diff**. A visible annotation indicates **92x** scaling from X-Cell to X-Cell-Ultra.

Main visible finding: the figure presents X-Cell as a large-scale single-cell perturbation foundation model trained on multi-screen atlas data, designed for perturbation prediction and biological generalization, with X-Cell-Ultra shown as substantially larger than X-Cell.

figure_candidates.caption: Fig. 2 X-Atlas/Pisces enables identification of context-dependent and context-independent perturbations. (A) Distribution of median UMIs per cell (top), median genes per cell (middle), and median on-target KD % (bottom) across GEMs for each screen in X-Atlas/Pisces. Black lines indicate median. (B) Recall of annotated gene pairs from CORUM (left) and STRING (right), calculated across all possible subsets of 1-7 screens. Error bars represent standard deviation across subsets. (C) Schematic of binary classifier for classifying perturbed cells from non-targeting controls (NTCs) (left). Input is a balanced mixture of perturbed cells for a given perturbation and NTCs. Model is logistic regression with L1-penalization (LASSO). Outputs are significance of the perturbation as measured by a one-sided binomial test and the features (genes) used to make the prediction. Percentage of perturbed cells with a significant phenotype (FDR < 0.05) as measured by a LASSO binary classifier (right). (D) Heatmap of F1 scores for perturbations in X-Atlas/Pisces clustered based on F1 scores across screens. Rows represent perturbations (n=6,412) that pass the following filtering criteria: (1) present in ≥ 3 screens, (2) ≥ 10 cells in each screen the perturbation was present in, (3) significant phenotype (FDR < 0.05) in at least 1 screen, and (4) F1 score ≥ 0.75 in at least 1 screen. Grey represents absence of a perturbation in that screen. Columns represent screens that are hierarchically clustered by similarity in F1 scores (colorbar). (E) Mean F1 score versus mean Jaccard index for perturbations across screens. Points are colored by F1 score coefficient of variation (CV) (colorbar). (F) UMAP of significant perturbations with at least one non-self feature (n=35,016) colored by screen. Clusters are labeled with CORUM complex enrichments, colored black if ≤ 50% of perturbations are from any individual screen, or the majority screen color otherwise. Inset structures of representative protein complexes are color-coded by whether the protein is targeted by a genetic perturbation in the indicated clusters (green shades are present, gray is absent).

(E) Heatmaps show the log 2 fold change in expression of APPL2 in D2 (left) and D3 (right) 48 hours post-stimulation as observed by the data and predicted by STATE, X-Cell, and X-Cell-Ultra.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure combining model/workflow schematic and quantitative benchmark plots for “X-Cell-Ultra.”

Panel A shows a workflow/model diagram: perturbation data from cell lines and iPSC-derived cell types, pre-training, and genome-scale zero-shot inference for primary human T cells, including “test-time adaptation” with frozen cross-attention/reduced learning rate.

Panel B shows model scaling dynamics: scatter/line plot of test loss versus trainable parameters for Replogle-Nadig, with Pearson r color scale, plus inset line plots comparing X-Cell and X-Cell-Ultra across epochs for Pearson correlation and differential expression Pearson correlation.

Panels C and D show benchmark results with histograms and bar/box plots for Pearson Δ, differential expression direction match, and MAE. Labels include melanocyte progenitor test perturbations, D2/D3 rest and stimulation contexts, and baselines such as control mean, perturbation mean, STATE, X-Cell, and X-Cell-Ultra.

Panel E shows clustered heatmaps of log fold-change values for APPL2 under D2 and D3 stimulation at 48 hours, comparing STATE, X-Cell, X-Cell-Ultra, and measured stimulation conditions.

Main visible finding: X-Cell-Ultra generally improves predictive performance, with higher Pearson/direction-match metrics and lower MAE than X-Cell or baseline methods, and shows improved scaling with larger trainable parameter counts.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

UMAP scatter plot of single-cell data with axes labeled UMAP1 and UMAP2. Points are colored by annotated cell type/state, with a legend including Epithelial Ectoderm, Mesenchymal Fibroblast, Mesenchymal Progenitor, Neural Crest/EMT, Neural Crest/Melanocyte Progenitor, Neuroectoderm, Neuron, and cycling states G2M, S-phase, and Stress Response.

The plot shows distinct cell populations forming separated clusters, including a large epithelial ectoderm cluster on the left and multiple neural/mesenchymal/cycling-related clusters on the right, indicating transcriptionally distinct cell states or lineages in the sampled cells.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure with quantitative plots and network visualizations.

Panels:
- **A**: Bar plots comparing recall of biological networks for **CORUM** and **StringDB**, and number of cells across **HCT116 full**, **2 screens**, and **3 screens** conditions. Recall increases with more screens.
- **B**: Bar plots of cluster-level specificity scores: **non-context specificity**, **HepG2 specificity**, and **iPSC specificity**. Bars are shown for clusters 0-9, with highlighted high-specificity clusters.
- **C**: Large labeled network/embedding visualization with many colored gene or complex labels and connecting edges, likely showing biological modules or protein complexes.
- **D**: Spatial/network plot colored by **Gini coefficient** with a green-to-red legend from 0 to 1, showing heterogeneous cluster/module specificity across the graph.
- **E**: Comparison plot of **mean STRING combined score** for **shuffled** versus **observed** groups, with many faint connecting lines and labeled points; observed scores appear higher than shuffled for many complexes.

Main visible finding: integrating multiple screens improves biological network recall, and the identified clusters/modules show context-specific biological structure and stronger observed STRING associations than shuffled controls.

figure_candidates.caption: Supplementary Figure 3 Performance comparison between STATE models trained on different datasets and X-Cell. For a fair comparison, we trained STATE (Pisces) model on a dataset set matching that used to train the X-Cell model, and STATE replogle on all publicly available datasets. We evaluate performance using six metrics across iPSC and HepG2 cell lines.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel bar plot comparing methods on the `iPSC-200` dataset. Panels show metrics labeled `Overlap@N ↑`, `DE Direction Match ↑`, `DE Spearman LFC ↑`, `Pearson Δ ↑`, `MAE ↓`, and `Discrimination L2 ↑`. Each panel has three colored bars for `STATE (Replogle+VCC)`, `STATE (Pisces)`, and `X-Cell`.

Visible values indicate X-Cell is highest for DE direction match (~0.915), DE Spearman LFC (~0.915), Pearson Δ (~0.510), and Discrimination L2 (~0.553), tied or near-tied on Overlap@N (~0.306), and lowest/best on MAE (~0.026). The plot presents benchmarking results where X-Cell generally outperforms the two STATE baselines across most metrics.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel bar chart comparing three models or methods: **STATE (Replogle+VCC)**, **STATE (Pisces)**, and **x-Cell** for **HepG2-200**.

Panels/metrics shown left to right:
- **Overlap@N ↑**
- **DE Direction Match ↑**
- **DE Spearman LFC ↑**
- **Pearson Δ ↑**
- **MAE ↓**
- **Discrimination L2 ↑**

Each panel has three colored bars with numeric values above them. The main visible finding is that **x-Cell** performs best on most upward metrics, especially **DE Direction Match**, **DE Spearman LFC**, **Pearson Δ**, and **Discrimination L2**, and has the lowest **MAE**. STATE variants are lower on most metrics, though close to each other for several DE-related measures.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific results figure with plots summarizing perturbation/pathway analyses across modalities.

Panel A: clustered heatmap titled “Attention weights per perturbation,” with rows for modalities `ESM2`, `StringDB`, `GenePT`, `DepMap`, `CellPainting`, and `scGPT`; columns are `380 perturbations`. A red color scale indicates attention weight, approximately 0.00 to 0.32. A dendrogram clusters perturbations across the top.

Panel B: bar chart titled “Total significant pathways per modality,” y-axis “Total significant pathways,” x-axis “Modality.” Bars show StringDB highest at 94, scGPT 80, GenePT 44, ESM2 42, DepMap 38, and CellPainting 13.

Panel C: heatmap titled “Significant MSigDB_Hallmark Pathways per Perturbation × Modality,” with modalities as rows and perturbations/pathway labels densely shown on the x-axis. Red intensity indicates significance or count/enrichment strength per modality-perturbation combination.

Main visible finding: StringDB and scGPT contribute the largest numbers of significant pathways, while CellPainting contributes the fewest; attention weights vary strongly by modality and perturbation, with StringDB and scGPT showing consistently higher attention in Panel A.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing a model/workflow and quantitative results.

Panel A: Schematic model architecture for “Perturbation Conditioning,” with control encoding using gene embedding, expression value, and diffusion model encoder feeding a Q × KV attention mechanism. Prior knowledge sources are shown as StringDB, DepMap, and ESM2, with cross-attention every 3 layers of self-attention and a batch-inference output. Labels mention knowledge-base importance and TCR pathway enrichment for top 1,000 genes with highest attention scores.

Panel B: Bar plot titled “Change in Attention Scores of TCR Signaling Pathway Genes.” Y-axis shows relative change in contribution, arbitrary scale. Methods on the x-axis include StringDB, scGPT, CellPainting, ESM2, GenePT, and DepMap. GenePT, ESM2, and DepMap show positive increases, while StringDB, scGPT, and CellPainting show decreases.

Panel C: Bar plot titled “Over-representation of the Top 1,000 Genes in TCR Signaling Pathway.” Y-axis is odds ratio. Bars compare GenePT, ESM2, DepMap, CellPainting, scGPT, and StringDB, with a dashed reference line at odds ratio 1. Legend indicates dark outlines for p-value < 0.05 and light outlines for p-value ≥ 0.05. GenePT, ESM2, and DepMap show stronger enrichment than the other methods.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Two-panel statistical plot showing model/experiment performance by cell line group. The left panel is a box/strip plot for **MAE (lower better ↓)** with y-axis values around 0.065–0.090 and x-axis groups **Similar (Training-like)** and **Distant** under **Cell Line Group**; the Similar group has lower MAE than Distant, with an annotated significance label **p = 0.005 \*\***. The right panel is a box/strip plot for **Pearson Δ (higher better ↑)** comparing the same groups; Similar has higher Pearson Δ than Distant, with **p = 0.026 \***. Points, boxplots, and highlighted diamond markers are visible, indicating distributions and central tendency.

figure_candidates.caption: Supplementary Figure 7 Architecture ablations, training efficiency, and scaling analysis for X-Cell-Ultra. (A) Architecture and loss ablation on the 4.9B model (Replogle-Nadig, 6 epochs). Scatter shows δ -norm ratio ˆ ρ vs. DE Pearson r for six configurations; color = MAE. The red shaded region (ˆ ρ < 0 . 2) indicates conservative collapse (predicting small effects). Replacing scale-invariant losses with CCC and removing the hidden residual shortcut progressively recovered both magnitude (ˆ ρ : 0 . 22 → 0 . 51) and direction (DEr : 0 . 05 → 0 . 33); see Table A1. (B) Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) comparison. X-Cell-Ultra achieves 41% MFU on 64 H200 GPUs, comparable to Llama 3 (reported 38-43% [95]) and ∼ 20 × the 55M X-Cell (2%). (C) Normalized loss scaling (relative to 83M model). Both train (dashed, α = 0 . 32, R 2 = 0 . 96) and test (solid, α = 0 . 03, R 2 = 0 . 97) follow power laws; color = DE Pearson r . (D) Individual validation metrics vs. trainable parameters: centroid accuracy (left) and per-perturbation MAE (right), colored by validation loss. (E) Training dynamics over 20 epochs: test loss (left) and DE Pearson r (right) for all five model sizes.
vlm_descriptions:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel experimental result figure with plots comparing model scaling and evaluation metrics. Panels A-E show scatter plots, bar charts, and training curves.

Panel A: Scatter plot of `δ-norm ratio (ρ)` versus `DE Pearson r`, with points labeled by normalization/architecture variants such as “60M baseline,” “MLP head,” “CCC+dmp (residual),” “Tied + QK-Norm,” and “add tied.” Color legend indicates `MAE`.

Panel B: Horizontal bar chart of `Model FLOPs Utilization (%)`, comparing models including `scGPT`, `X-CELL`, `Llama 3`, and `X-Cell-Ultra`, with parameter counts and percentage annotations.

Panel C: Scaling plot of `Normalized Loss (relative to 83M)` versus `Trainable Parameters`, with colored points for model sizes from `83M` to `3.1B`; legend/colorbar indicates `DE Pearson r`. Train and test trend lines are shown.

Panel D: Two scaling scatter plots: left shows `Control Accuracy` versus `Trainable Parameters`; right shows `Per-gene MAE` versus `Trainable Parameters`, with model sizes labeled and color indicating validation loss.

Panel E: Training curves over `Epoch` for different model sizes. Left plot shows `Test Loss` decreasing with training; right plot shows `DE Pearson r` increasing over epochs.

Main visible finding: larger trainable models generally improve performance, with lower loss/per-gene MAE and higher DE Pearson correlation/control accuracy, while the largest models around 1.6B-3.1B parameters appear strongest across several metrics.
